articles.title: MIT affiliates named 2026 Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Fellows
articles.content: Five MIT faculty members and two additional alumni were recently named to the 2026 cohort of AI2050 Fellows. The honor is announced annually by Schmidt Sciences, Eric and Wendy Schmidt’s philanthropic initiative that aims to accelerate scientific innovation. Conceived and co-chaired by Eric Schmidt and James Manyika, AI2050 is a philanthropic initiative aimed at helping to solve hard problems in artificial intelligence . Within their research, each fellow will contend with the central motivating question of AI2050: “It’s 2050. AI has turned out to be hugely beneficial to society. What happened? What are the most important problems we solved and the opportunities and possibilities we realized to ensure this outcome?” AI2050 Senior Fellow Sendhil Mullainathan is the Peter de Florez Professor at MIT with dual appointments in the departments of Economics and Electrical Engineering and Computer Science who is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. His current research is at the intersection of algorithms and people, with a central focus on launching The Bike Shop@MIT , a new research center that works toward more human-centered AI through scalable bicycles for the mind, and innovative new gears for machine learning algorithms. Mullainathan is the co-founder of ideas42, a nonprofit to apply behavioral science; MIT's Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, which promotes the use of randomized control trials in development; and Dandelion Health , which combines proprietary AI tools with real-world patient data. He's the co-author of "Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much." Among other awards, he is a recipient of the MacArthur “Genius Grant”; has been designated a “Young Global Leader” by the World Economic Forum; was labeled a “Top 100 Thinker” by Foreign Policy Magazine; and was named to the “Smart List: 50 people who will change the world” by Wired Magazine (U.K.). He serves on the board of the MacArthur Foundation, is affiliated with the NBER and BREAD, and is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. His AI2050 project focuses on the translation of patterns detectable by AI into testable theories. AI2050 Early Career Fellows Alex Damian is an assistant professor in the Department of Mathematics, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, who is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. His research focuses on the mathematical foundations of deep learning, with an emphasis on optimization dynamics and representation learning. He was previously a research fellow at the Kempner Institute at Harvard University. He received his PhD in applied and computational mathematics from Princeton University and his BS in mathematics from Duke University. His AI2050 project focuses on effective AI model training. Bailey Flanigan is a Theodore T. Miller (1922) Career Development Assistant Professor at MIT, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the departments of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and Political Science, and is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. She received her PhD in computer science from Carnegie Mellon University in 2024. In 2024-25, she was a Harvard Data Science Initiative Fellow, hosted at the Harvard Ash Center for Democratic Innovation. Her research combines tools from across disciplines (including social choice theory, game theory, algorithms, statistics, and survey methods) to advance political methodology and strengthen public participation in democracy. She is specifically interested in sampling algorithms, opinion measurement/preference elicitation, and the design of democratic innovations like deliberative minipublics and participatory budgeting. articles.title: Anthropic just removed one of Claude’s biggest usage limits — but not for everyone
articles.content: Claude Code users on Anthropic’s $200 plan will no longer face a rolling five-hour usage cap , provided their accounts are verified and they have weekly usage left. Anthropic announced the change Friday as it renamed its two top consumer plans. Max 5x is now Max, and Max 20x becomes Ultra. They still cost $100 and $200 a month, respectively, and current subscribers don’t need to do anything to switch. Max 5x is now Max, and Max 20x becomes Ultra. Anthropic’s pricing page also lists monthly Claude Platform API credits: $100 with Max and $200 with Ultra. That adds another consideration for developers who use Claude Code while building applications against the API, with each plan bundling API credits equal to its monthly subscription price. Claude Code creator Boris Cherny highlighted the limit change in his own post . What the five-hour cap meant The five-hour limit capped usage within a rolling window, and a demanding task could burn through that allowance much sooner. Claude Code users could hit it midway through debugging or a large refactor and have to wait for a reset despite having weekly usage left. Verification comes first Some Ultra subscribers will have to wait for Anthropic to verify their accounts before the five-hour limit goes away. The company says the checks help prevent fraud and abuse, and it will email users when the cap is lifted. Some Ultra subscribers will have to wait for Anthropic to verify their accounts before the five-hour limit goes away. According to Anthropic’ , verification happens automatically based on account and payment history. There’s no way to request it or speed it up so some users will just have to be patient. The weekly cap remains Ultra users still have the same weekly allowance, and they could use it up sooner without the five-hour limit forcing them to pause. The pricing page lists Ultra at 10 times Pro’s weekly usage, compared with five times Pro’s weekly usage on Max. The pricing page lists Ultra at 10 times Pro’s weekly usage, compared with five times Pro’s weekly usage on Max. Your chats with Claude count toward the same weekly limit as your Claude Code sessions, whether you’re on the web, desktop, or mobile. Once you use up that allowance, you can turn on usage credits to keep working at standard API rates, though you’ll pay extra on top of your subscription. If you keep hitting the session limit with weekly usage to spare, avoiding those interruptions could make Ultra worth the extra $100 a month over Max, but if you already run out before the week is over, removing the session cap won’t give you more included usage. OpenAI eases its limits A day earlier, OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux announced higher usage limits for Pro subscribers and Business Premium. OpenAI also dropped a planned cut for existing $200 Pro subscribers after customers objected. In a separate pricing decision, the company abandoned an idea to replace token-based billing with flat per-job fees after developers pushed back. The post Anthropic just removed one of Claude’s biggest usage limits — but not for everyone appeared first on The New Stack .

articles.title: Nvidia store quietly pulls the RTX 5080 following RTX 5090 removal — street prices climb to 2.2X over MSRP
articles.content: First, it was the GeForce RTX 5090 , and now the GeForce RTX 5080 – two of the best graphics cards have gone dark. After the Blackwell flagship left Nvidia's marketplace, the GeForce RTX 5080 followed suit. Prices for the sub-flagship have exploded to more than 2.2X its original $999 MSRP, and the Blackwell-powered graphics card is slowly going out of stock at various U.S. retailers. As with the recent disappearance of the GeForce RTX 5090 on Nvidia’s marketplace, the listings and filters for the GeForce RTX 5080 have also disappeared. While its absence does not necessarily mean Nvidia has discontinued the graphics card, it does raise questions about its status and future availability. This move is especially fishy because other Blackwell SKUs, such as the GeForce RTX 5070 Ti and GeForce RTX 5070 , remain listed on the marketplace, albeit marked as “Out of Stock.” The continued presence of the GeForce RTX 5070 Ti and GeForce RTX 5070 suggests that Nvidia wants to keep the products visible even when they are not immediately available so that consumers can anticipate restocks. The complete removal of the GeForce RTX 5090 and GeForce RTX 5080 breaks that pattern. It fuels rumors that Nvidia has allegedly stopped production of the GeForce RTX 5090 and possibly the GeForce RTX 5080 too, in favor of a rumored GeForce RTX 5080 24GB. (Image credit: Nvidia) Rumors claim Nvidia allegedly stopped producing the GeForce RTX 5090 to repurpose the valuable GB202 silicon into the chipmaker’s RTX Pro Blackwell lineup, which fetches higher margins. This has a lot of credence, since many agree that Nvidia stopped being a gaming hardware vendor long ago and has transformed into an AI provider. Rather than simply discontinuing the GeForce RTX 5090, Nvidia purportedly intends to introduce the GeForce RTX 5080 24GB as the new flagship gaming graphics card. The thing is, a 24GB variant of the GeForce RTX 5080 would solve one of the biggest consumer gripes with the graphics card: the lack of memory. While a GeForce RTX 5080 24GB would offer the same memory as the GeForce RTX 5090, it simply isn't a direct drop-in replacement. The former has 2X fewer CUDA cores, a substantial performance gap that even a 50% memory increase can't make up for. How much money are you willing to spend during the Black Friday sales? The GeForce RTX 5080 launched in January of last year with an MSRP of $999. Demand quickly outpaced supply, and with the rapid price hikes due to the memory shortage, the market price has more than doubled its original MSRP. As of this moment, the most affordable GeForce RTX 5080 in stock, the PNY GeForce RTX 5080 ARGB Epic-X RGB OC, retails for $2,199.99 , which is 2.2X over the original launch price. While some stock remains, it’s selling out fast, and the remaining units will only get more expensive as availability dwindles. At this rate, the GeForce RTX 5080 is unlikely to be available by Black Friday. If you are set on a GeForce RTX 5080, you may have little choice but to act quickly and buy at today's elevated prices. If the GeForce RTX 5080 24GB is indeed legitimate, the graphics card will almost certainly debut at a substantial premium over the original GeForce RTX 5080. Although Nvidia maintains that the RTX 5090 is still alive, the reality suggests otherwise. We have contacted the company for comment regarding the GeForce RTX 5080’s status.

articles.title: Intel’s woes wipe out $1 trillion of semiconductor market cap in one day — PC market bloodbath leaves few chip stocks unscathed
articles.content: Intel's shares plunged 30% on Friday, wiping out nearly $150 billion in market capitalization in a single day, the largest single-day loss in the company's history. The decline followed a disappointing financial outlook, largely driven by an anticipated drop of more than 20% in sales at Intel's client computing group (CCPG), the company's main cash cow. The declines quickly spread across the semiconductor industry. Although losses elsewhere were nowhere near as severe as Intel's, approximately $1 trillion in semiconductor market capitalization was wiped out on Friday, according to intraday estimates by Benzinga . Fire sale The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index (SOX), which tracks the stock performance of 30 major semiconductor companies, is one of the key indicators of the industry's financial health. On Friday, the index plunged 9.14%, or 1,052.82 points, to 10,465.38 points as of 2:31 PM ET, as Intel's disappointing outlook triggered a massive selloff across the semiconductor industry. Intel was by far the biggest loser, as other chip-related stocks, while Arm (-12.68%), AMD (-12.48%), Qualcomm (-12.14%), Applied Materials (-8.73%), ASML (-8.13%), Lam Research (-8%), Micron (-7.28%), and Broadcom (-7.1%) suffered considerably less. Then again, while Nvidia lost 5.66% of its market cap, this translates to around $270 billion, which is a massive amount of money. Paradoxically, Nvidia lost more market capitalization in absolute dollar terms than Intel. Reuters noted that investors increasingly question the scale of capital investments required to expand AI infrastructure as well as the sustainability of that spending. Gloomy outlook Intel’s client computing and physical AI group (CCPG) generated $8.1 billion in revenue during Q3 2026, down 5% year-over-year and 9% sequentially. Weaker demand and increased competition reduced client processor shipments by 14% year-over-year, which was partially offset by a 9% increase in average selling prices. CCPG accounted for nearly half of Intel's revenue of around $16.5 billion and the company's main source of cash. As strong demand for server processors only partially offsets declining client sales, Intel guided its Q4 revenue to be between $15 billion and $16 billion. Intel expects the client market to deteriorate further in Q4 2026 and into 2027 as elevated memory prices and shortages of other components impact PC prices and demand. In general, Intel expects the client PC market to decline 10% in 2027 compared to 2026, which will inevitably have an effect on CCPG performance. While Intel expects its data center business to continue growing in 2027, industry-wide supply constraints will limit its ability to fully capitalize on demand. 2026 has been a mixed bag for Intel so far. On the one hand, the company achieved its highest market capitalization ever — $673.43 billion in mid-June — on growing sales of data center CPUs, strong sales of client products, and a return to profitability (if the $12.5 billion non-cash accounting charge associated with shares issued to the U.S. government is excluded). articles.title: iPhone demand sees Apple topple Nvidia as most valuable company, again
articles.content: Tech stocks have been a bloodbath this last week, but Apple's iPhone has supported the company enough with it once more taking the top spot as the most valuable firm in the world. Apple's valuation is down, but the largest in the world That top spot has been going back and forth between Apple and Nvidia for some time now, as iPhone and Services demand go up against AI chip consumption. This time, Apple's stock has been rising on the back of multiple hardware releases, plus the seamless transition of CEO from Tim Cook to John Ternus . Apple stock closed on October 30 down to $344.63, leaving the company with a $5.03 trillion valuation. Nvidia had a tough day too, and finished below AAPL at $204.64 per share, and a $4.93 trillion valuation. This latest valuation comes despite one analyst believing that Apple has confused iPhone buyers. Loop Capital claims that moving the base iPhone launch from September to some point early in 2027 has left buyers unsure. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: Android Auto can run sideloaded apps for free with this new tool
articles.content: Credit: Andy Walker / Android Authority TL;DR Someone has created a tool called UnknownAuto that lets self-built or sideloaded apps run on Android Auto. The tool marks the app as “installed from Google Play,” so Android Auto accepts it. UnknownAuto is billed as a free, open-source alternative to AA Enabler. Android Auto can run a large variety of apps, but not every app. The platform refuses to run apps that have been sideloaded. If there was ever an app you wished could run on Android Auto but doesn’t, there may be a solution. One user, who goes by u/mannumaster on Reddit, says they wanted to build their own app and use it on Android Auto. When they ran into roadblocks, they created a new tool called UnknownAuto. This tool is free, open-sourced, and can work offline. The creator describes it as an alternative to the proprietary AA Enabler.

articles.title: Busy GPUs can hide slow AI inference on Kubernetes
articles.content: A Kubernetes cluster can be healthy while the AI service running on it disappoints users. A model might return its first token quickly but take too long to finish an answer. It might respond promptly and still give the wrong answer. And a busy GPU tells the operations team little about either outcome. The operational challenge is connecting AI service behavior with the Kubernetes, GPU, compute, storage, and network conditions behind it—not viewing each layer in isolation. That’s why you should measure an inference service before production, then compare live behavior with the baseline. In the fourth article in this HPE-sponsored series on AI and Kubernetes, The New Stack speaks with Marius Bogoevici , Senior Principal Product Manager for HPE Morpheus Software; Mahesh Ramachandran , Vice President of Product Management for HPE OpsRamp Software ; and Karthik Subramanian , Principal Product Manager for HPE Morpheus Software . Inference adds a further question: Does the whole service deliver a useful result at a cost and speed the business can support? Earlier in this series: Part 1: Developers and platform teams both want Kubernetes self-service. They disagree on who owns it. Part 2: A live Kubernetes cluster can still have an ownership gap Part 3: Your Kubernetes dashboard is green. Your users are seeing red. Start with the experience, then establish a baseline For a conversational service, Bogoevici recommends measuring time to first token, time per output token, reliability, capacity, resource efficiency, cost, and answer quality. The right mix depends on the experience a team intends to deliver. A quick first token can mask slow subsequent generation; a fast complete response can still be inaccurate or unhelpful. “A quick first token can mask slow subsequent generation; a fast complete response can still be inaccurate or unhelpful.” Time to first token and time to a complete response answer different questions. Inter-token latency and time per output token help explain generation speed after the first token arrives. Teams should document where they measure each interval and compare results under sustained load and demand spikes. Set targets for the particular workload and user experience. Ramachandran urges teams to profile the AI serving system before customers depend on it. Test representative prompt and context lengths, output volumes, and traffic levels. Record token throughput, latency, and service-level measures under those conditions. The resulting baseline gives operators a reference to measure production behavior changes. Correlating those workload measures with infrastructure performance and capacity helps teams distinguish rising inference demand from resource contention and plan capacity more effectively. As Ramachandran tells The New Stack , teams should “profile it before you launch.” Quality needs its own evaluation. Bogoevici says teams should ask whether the service gives proper answers or hallucinates. Platform telemetry can show a request was served, but data science and domain specialists need representative tests and acceptance criteria for the answer. The newly published ebook, Kubernetes in 2027: Building platforms for AI, autonomy, and scale , recommends assessing output quality alongside service performance and revisiting both after model, prompt, retrieval, or serving changes. When the GPU is busy but the service is slow GPU utilization is a useful signal, but it does not identify the bottleneck . Bogoevici sketches a misleading victory lap: “Our GPUs are maxed at 100%. So we’re doing well.” That tells teams little about how the service actually performs. Ramachandran suggests checking whether inference pods scale on workload-appropriate metrics, whether requests reach the intended model, and whether related components can be scheduled when needed. Different models can have different latency and capacity demands, so a change in request mix can…

articles.title: Over 300 Chrome extensions found hijacking searches of 13.4 million users — how to stay safe
articles.content: An ongoing security investigation by Socket's John Tuckner (via Bleeping Computer ) has discovered a search-hijacking campaign that involves 319 Chrome extensions with a combined 13.4 million downloads. The malicious extensions redirect search queries through tracking servers to generate advertising revenue from Bing and Yahoo. It's more than double from Tuckner's April report that found "only" 57 Chrome extensions and 6 million downloads. According to Tuckner, the malicious extensions are usually found on websites advertising tools that are labeled as "PDF converter", "AI search", or "safe search". "These extensions were created by a handful of organized operators all working from the same idea: quietly take over the browser's default search engine, route every query through a suspicious proxy server, and collect partner referral payments from Yahoo or Bing under a syndication partner ID," Tuckner wrote. The extensions apparently aren't found on the official Chrome Web Store either. Rather, they're unlisted and are only really found through the shady advertising. How the extensions work (Image credit: Shutterstock) Apparently, the extensions use Chrome's built-in 'chrome_settings_override' setting that lets them replace your default search provider. What this means is that your searches are captured as they pass through the operator's server. After that the redirect could be sent through a site with malware attached, though currently, per Tuckner they're mostly routing to Yahoo and Bing and to falsely claim advertising revenue. "The search referral revenue is a profitable watering hole while the proxy operator can wait for data to accumulate and targets to surface before redirecting to malicious search results or landing pages for phishing or other malicious downloads," Tuckner said. As of this writing, the report says that most of the extensions have been removed the Chrome Web Store when the report was published, however, new ones are constantly being added. "Ultimately, Google can benefit from more advertisements being run and more extensions being listed in the marketplace so there may not be an urgent reason to police this activity too broadly." How to stay safe (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Even if Google isn't policing this specific type of extension, malicious add-ons do slip through to the Chrome Web Store from time to time. When it comes to extensions, you need to be extra careful when downloading and adding them to your browser. Normally, we would recommend you stick to well-known extensions from trusted brands. However, sometimes a lone developer creates one that does exactly what you need. There are several recommendations we have to help you be a bit safer. Check the ratings and reviews of the extensions but also dig into the developer to see if they're legit. Look, even good extensions can go bad , so you want to make sure that your Windows PC is protected with the best antivirus software and that you’re using the best Mac antivirus software on your Apple computer. That way, if an extension is spreading malware or other viruses, they’ll be detected and stopped before they can do any damage. If you're constantly trying different extensions, you should consider one of the best identity theft protection services . They can help get your identity back if it's stolen or recover lost funds due to scams and cyberattacks. articles.title: Dell's 15 touchscreen laptop with 1TB of storage is the office machine I’d recommend to remote workers — especially now it's $300 off at Best Buy
articles.content: In our experience, when it comes to business laptops you can't really go wrong with a Dell. But while the likes of the XPS dominate the high-end, I'm not convinced most professionals need a machine like that. For remote and hybrid workers the Dell 15 laptop for $900 (was $1200) at Best Buy , is an easy pick for productivity that doesn't compromise on power for general office work, emails, video calls, and - of course - streaming movies in your downtime. For me, laptop checks every box and gives you plenty of room for files. • Best for: students, families, and home workers who want a dependable, big-screen everyday laptop with lots of storage. • Why we like it: a 15.3-inch touchscreen with 400 nits of brightness, a generous 1TB SSD, 16GB of memory for smooth multitasking, a backlit keyboard, and a light 3.34-pound design. 15 (Core 7 350): was $1199.99 now $899.99 A 15.3-inch laptop with a 1920 x 1200 IPS touchscreen rated at 400 nits, Intel’s Core 7 350 processor from its new Core Series 3 lineup, integrated Intel graphics, 16GB of memory, a 1TB SSD, a backlit keyboard, HDMI 2.1, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Windows 11. It weighs 3.34 pounds and comes in Celestial Blue. View Deal Why we recommend it Dell’s mainstream laptops have long been a safe pick for anyone who wants a reliable machine without paying for premium extras, and the 2026 Dell 15 brings a thinner, lighter design and Intel’s new Core Series 3 chips. We haven’t tested it yet, although we've reviewed plenty of similar models from Dell, and have a couple in use at home precisely as WFH machines. The specs are great here, and the 1TB SSD stands out, since most laptops at this price still ship with 512GB. Price Context & Historical Value This is $300, or 25%, off Best Buy’s $1,199.99 comparison price, but since this model just launched, there’s little price history to compare it to. Personally, I think the $1,199.99 list price flatters the discount. Still, $899.99 for 16GB of RAM, 1TB of storage, and a touchscreen is a fair price given how much memory costs have climbed this year. It’s a sensible buy if you need a laptop, but it may well get cheaper as Black Friday nears. Should You Buy It? ✅ Buy the Dell 15 (2026) if... you want a reliable office laptop with a big touchscreen, need plenty of storage for photos and files, or want a light machine that’s easy to carry around the home office, into work, or to class. ❌ Skip the Dell 15 (2026) if... you need a laptop capable of graphics-intensive workloads, as that's beyond what this Dell machine can handle. Check out all laptop deals at Best Buy .

articles.title: A Claude model autonomously chose a gene therapy and operated on a mouse brain with no human decision-making
articles.content: An AI agent performed brain surgery on an epileptic mouse, picking the drug, the brain target, and the injection coordinates on its own. According to lead researcher Ocana-Santero, it's the first time an AI agent has autonomously chosen a treatment and delivered it to a living mammal. But when a calibration error hit mid-surgery, the agent refused to continue and couldn't be talked out of it. The article A Claude model autonomously chose a gene therapy and operated on a mouse brain with no human decision-making appeared first on The Decoder .

articles.title: 14 New Things Your iPhone Can Do in iOS 27.2
articles.content: Apple released iOS 27.2 on October 26, bringing enhancements to Siri AI, adding Suggestions in Messages, and sneaking in a string of smaller additions across Photos, Podcasts, Games, Apple TV, and FaceTime. iOS 27.2 is available to download to your device now via Settings ➝ General ➝ Software Update. Note that some features may not be available in all regions or on all iPhone models. Apple maintains a feature availability list with all the details. Ask Siri About Past Conversations Siri AI can now recall your past conversations, so you can ask it about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week. Siri AI features require an iPhone 16 model or later, or an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 15 Pro Max. Get Answers From More of Your Personal Context Siri AI can now draw from more sources when answering, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, and your voicemails. Apple says you'll also get better results from Safari history and Reading List. Use Siri in More Languages Siri AI now supports French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, in addition to English. Just keep in mind that, as things stand, it's not available in the EU or mainland China. Control Which Apps Siri and Search Can Access A new settings menu has been added that lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one list. You can find it in Settings ➝ Siri ➝ Excluded Apps. Copy Just Part of a Siri Response Granular text selection lets you select and copy only the part of a Siri response you need, rather than the whole reply. Act on Suggestions in Messages The new Suggestions in Messages feature aims to help you take quick actions based on the context of a conversation, like adding a Calendar invite for a dinner or saving a Reminder. The feature appeared during iOS 27 beta testing but was held back from the initial release , so its arrival has been a good while coming. Manage Shared Albums More Easily Shared Albums in Photos gain three additions. You can now edit captions and comments, the app can avoid adding duplicate photos, and it can display a reminder before an album expires so participants can save important photos and videos. Spot AI-Generated Images iOS 27.2 supports SynthID watermarking, which aims to help you identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground. See What Your Friends Are Playing In the Games app, the Friends tab now provides context around friend suggestions, plus it shows you any recent games your friends have played on their player pages. Create Apple TV Profiles for Your Household If you have an Apple TV, you can now create profiles in the account settings section on iPhone and iPad. All you need for a profile is a name, plus whether it's for an adult or a child. Creating a profile for a child limits content to a PG rating by default, but there's a customize option for finer control. You can select age ratings for TV shows and movies that are appropriate for the child based on their age. Stream FaceTime From Front and Rear Cameras Dual Capture is now available in group ‌FaceTime‌ calls, so you can stream ‌FaceTime‌ video content from the front and rear cameras at the same time. On a compatible device running ‌iOS 27‌.2, flipping the camera while on a ‌FaceTime‌ call automatically turns on Dual Capture. Dual Capture is available on the iPhone 17, ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro, ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro Max, iPhone Air, iPhone 18 Pro, ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max, and ‌iPhone Duo‌. Watch Several Live Sports Streams at Once Multiview has been expanded in the Apple TV app to the iPhone, so you can now watch up to four live sports streams at the same time. Multiview works for sports events that come with an ‌Apple TV‌ subscription, so that's Major League Soccer (MLS), Formula 1 (F1) in the U.S., and Friday Night Baseball doubleheaders during the Major League Baseball season. iPhone Duo Edge Light and Apple Pencil Support iOS 27.2 adds Apple…

articles.title: What worries Entire co-founder Thomas Dohmke about the future of tech?
articles.content: Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke is taking on his old company. His startup, Entire, launched a GitHub alternative this week , replacing traditional pull requests with Trails, a review system that uses AI agents to evaluate code changes while developers oversee the work. A month before that launch, The New Stack asked Dohmke what excites him most about technology’s future and what worries him. He welcomed the ability to turn more of his ideas into working software. His concern was about learning. “What worries me is that people think they no longer need to learn coding,” Entire’s co-founder and CEO told TNS at WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America in San Jose in September. “I think it’s fundamental for every kid out there to not only learn math and biology and geography, but also understand the basics of computer science.” “What worries me is that people think they no longer need to learn coding.” Dohmke was one of several people we posed those questions to at the conference. Their answers reveal enthusiasm for what more people can now build, along with some concerns about understanding, safety, and access to these new tools. For Josh Bentley , SAP’s senior director of community advocacy, broader access to technology means people can build things in hours or days that once took weeks or months. His concern: Whether that speed comes with enough understanding. “People are getting recognized as a builder when they really don’t understand the context of what they’re building,” Bentley said. Darko Mesaroš , distinguished developer advocate at AWS, was similarly excited about more people being able to build software. He also worried about bad code and “AI slop.” “I want people to be able to build more stuff, but I want people to build stuff more intentionally .” “I want people to be able to build more stuff, but I want people to build stuff more intentionally,” Mesaroš said. For Mark Cavage , Docker’s president and chief operating officer, the concern was whether the industry could quickly establish the safeguards and efficiencies needed around AI agents. “The thing that worries me about it, of course, is that actually we as an industry don’t figure out quickly enough how to bring ourselves new efficiencies and trust and safety around it,” Cavage said. Cassidy Williams , GitHub’s senior director of developer advocacy, was excited that people can ask a machine to help turn an idea into something real. She also raised concerns about safety guardrails and the cost of participating. Williams wants people to have accessible tools and “not be priced out from being able to be a part of the future.” The pace of change itself was a source of excitement for Matt Hobbs , head of Cloud, Engineering, Data, and AI at PwC. “Everything that I just built, I could rebuild again and do it better, do it faster, do it safer, do it more ready for enterprise scale,” Hobbs said. Frederic Branczyk , vice president of data engineering at Dash0, described his outlook as cautiously optimistic. He was excited about what AI enables his company to offer customers and how it uses the technology internally, while acknowledging the uncertainty ahead. “None of us really have the answers to all the problems that we’re facing together,” Branczyk said. The conversation is part of The New Stack ’s six-video Inside WeAreDevelopers series. The other five videos explore what developers should learn next, what teams are building, and what brings people together: What should every developer get hands-on with right now? — Speakers make the case for experimenting with GPU programming, local AI models, agent frameworks, and sandboxes. What people missed at WeAreDevelopers — From technical debates to unexpected career connections, attendees explain what…
articles.author: Nick Lucchesi

articles.title: This EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle is the home backup battery I’d keep ready for winter storms, and it’s $119 off at Best Buy
articles.content: EcoFlow has been a consistent top-performer in our tests, with one model earning the top spot in our guide to portable power stations. High-capacity, durable build, and reliable output are all strong with this line. So, the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic with 45W solar panel for $479 (was $598) at Best Buy is an easy recommendation. If a power outage leaves you without heat controls, internet, or a working fridge, the Delta 3 Classic gives you a quiet, fume-free backup you can keep indoors. • Best for: Professionals, campers, and RV owners who want dependable backup power for outages or portable power on the go. • Why we like it: Beyond the strong performance in our tests, this EcoFlow model features 1,024Wh of long-life LFP battery capacity, 1,800W of continuous AC output to run big appliances, 3,000 charge cycles, and a five-year warranty. The solar panels for off-grid use sweeten this one considerably for us. • What you need to know: At $479 it’s good value for the battery alone, though the small panel is more of a bonus for added energy security rather than a serious charging option. Delta 3 Classic: was $598 now $479 A 1,024Wh portable power station with a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery rated for 3,000 cycles, 1,800W of continuous AC output with a 3,600W peak, and a weight of 26.7 pounds. This bundle includes a 45W solar panel and a protective bag, and it comes with a five-year warranty. EcoFlow sells and ships it through Best Buy’s marketplace. View Deal Why We Recommend It EcoFlow is one of the biggest names in portable power, and the Delta 3 Classic is a pared-back version of its Delta 3 that keeps the essentials: a large, long-lasting LFP battery and enough output to run a full-size fridge or a space heater for a while. We haven’t tested this model ourselves, so this pick rests on EcoFlow’s track record and our experience testing other models. Expect fast charging, easy of use, and total dependability if you need additional or on-the-move power supply. The five-year warranty adds welcome peace of mind for a product you may rely on in an emergency. For more top picks, see our guide to the best portable power stations . Price Context & Historical Value This is $119, or 20%, off the bundle’s $598 list price, which is a solid discount on a 1kWh power station with a five-year warranty. Keep in mind that the included 45W panel would take more than a full day of ideal sunlight to refill the battery, so think of it as a top-up tool rather than a full-blown charging solution. If you want backup power in place before winter, this is a good time to buy. Should you buy it? ✅ Buy the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle if... you want reliable backup power for outages, you need enough output to run a fridge, router, or CPAP machine, or you value a long-life LFP battery with a five-year warranty. ❌ Skip the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle if... you plan to rely on solar charging, since a 45W panel is far too small to refill this battery quickly, you need a power station that’s easy to carry long distances at 26.7 pounds, or you’d prefer to buy directly from Best Buy rather than a marketplace seller. articles.title: HP's OmniBook X Flip 14 is a surprisingly high-end 2-in-1 touchscreen laptop with a mid-range price in Best Buy's latest sale
articles.content: If you want a laptop that doubles as a tablet for notes, streaming, and sketching without paying premium prices, the OmniBook X Flip delivers a lot for the money. The 2K touchscreen laptop comes equipped with a Core Ultra 5 226V chip that supports up to 40 NPU TOPS for general AI tasks. The 16GB LPDDR5 RAM, and 512GB SSD that makes it ideal for work, study, and downtime. Now, as part of Best Buy's Halloween Doorbuster sale, the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 is $649.99 (was $999.99) . Considering I see sluggish 8GB laptops selling for that price (and I urge you not to buy them), this is an easy recommendation. • Best for: students and professionals who want a stylish, versatile 2-in-1 for work, note-taking, and entertainment. • Why we like it: a sturdy all-metal 2-in-1 design, a high-resolution 14-inch touchscreen, efficient Intel Core Ultra 5 performance with Copilot+ AI features, and battery life that comfortably lasts a workday. OmniBook X Flip 4: was $999.99 now $649.99 A 14-inch 2-in-1 convertible with a 1920 x 1200 IPS touchscreen, an Intel Core Ultra 5 226V processor, 16GB of memory, a 512GB SSD, and Copilot+ PC features, finished in Atmospheric Blue. View Deal Why we recommend it While we haven't reviewed this specification, our sister site Tom’s Guide tested the exact configuration and found it a premium, durable 2-in-1 with a solid display, strong mid-range performance, and more than eight and a half hours of battery life. He did note that it comes loaded with bloatware you’ll want to remove, that the gapless keyboard takes some getting used to, and that the chassis warms up under heavy loads. Those are small trade-offs for a laptop that looks and feels far pricier than it is. Price Context & Historical Value This is $350, or 35%, off the $999.99 list price, but the OmniBook X Flip regularly sells well below that, and Tom’s Guide reviewed it when it was going for $599. That means $649.99 is a good price but not the lowest we’ve seen, and a newer Core Series 3 version is also listed alongside it. Buy now if you need a 2-in-1 today, but it may drop lower over Black Friday next month. Should You Buy It? ✅ Buy the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 if... you want a laptop that converts into a tablet for notes and streaming, you value a sturdy, premium-looking metal design, or you need battery life that lasts a full workday. ❌ Skip the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 if... you’d rather not spend time removing preinstalled bloatware, you prefer a traditional keyboard layout, or you’re willing to wait in case it drops back to $599 for Black Friday. articles.title: Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison thinks AI could make us all rich through a universal high income – but governments will need to change
articles.content: Speaking on-stage at the company's recent AI World conference, Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison declared AI could eventually make everyone "healthier and wealthier". Apparently unfazed by the technology's impacts on humanity, Ellison does acknowledge that governments need to have a shift in mindset to adapt to this new future. In a Q&A during the conference's hotly anticipated final keynote, Ellison outlined a future where AI systems and robots could dramatically reduce the cost of goods and services. But rather than accepting the suggestion that AI would end up replacing us all, he argued that the technology would ultimately serve to make us more productive, allowing workers to achieve things that simply weren't possible before. AI won't replace us, but it will change the economics of work in a lasting way "I think that's kind of nonsensical," Ellison said about predictions that AI will eventually replace everyone. The multi-billionaire accepted AI and automation will inevitably displace some jobs, pointing toward rideshare service s in a hint to ongoing approval of driverless cars in Las Vegas and other cities. But he also stressed not all jobs would be impacted equally, revealing his pilot qualifications on-stage and stressing that autopilot hasn't replaced human pilots despite being a decades-old technology. Although humans will continue to play supervisory roles in many industries (we're already seeing human knowledge worker roles evolve into AI agent managers in some cases), Ellison argued that the overall benefits would be positive, providing governments get involved to support the humans they represent. Painting a picture of what he meant, he described a hypothetical house being constructed entirely by robots in a scenario where automation had replaced human labor. Whereas human labor would have accounted for, say, 80% of the cost of a house before, four-fifths of the house instantly becomes cheaper because of the impact of automation. He used this example to set the foundation for the idea of 'universal high income' – a concept already floated by other tech billionaires, including Elon Musk. Taxation needs to change to enable the provision of a universal income "We need to change from taxing human labor to taxing value added," he said. "So when the robots add value, all that value that the robots add is taxed, and we could have universal high income." Universal high income is an evolution of the universal basic income concept, which provides citizens with a regular payment that covers essential living costs. Instead, he suggested that the enormous productivity gains that AI could eventually unlock could create enough wealth to support much higher incomes, despite declining human work activity. He referenced economist Milton Friedman's negative income tax proposal, describing it as a "reverse income tax" that could help distribute some of the wealth generated by AI. "The robots are adding value. The government's taxing the value... We all become wealthy as a result." However, Ellison's vision is a wildly ambitious one that would require a colossal change to today's systems. It would take more than a decade, he admitted. While a future of AI-induced human wealth with less work might sound far-fetched at best in today's economy, Ellison's optimism remains on track. "All of that is doable," he concluded. layoffs.fyi has tracked over 135,000 layoffs in the tech sector alone in 2026 to date, including around 21,000 Oracle workers in the 12 months between June 2025 and June 2026, and likely thousands more in September 2026 .

articles.title: Mozilla’s plan to rescue us from the zombie internet
articles.content: There is an uneasy feeling these days when surfing the web that the internet has irrevocably changed. Log on to social media and you’re wading through a sea of influencers psy-opping you into buying stuff you don’t need. Scroll through LinkedIn and you can barely tell whether a post was written by a human or generated by Claude to rack up clicks and likes. Everywhere you look, the internet feels a little less human—and increasingly, it is. Recent studies suggest that at least half of the content posted online is AI -generated. How then do we reclaim the internet as a space for genuine human connection and creativity? That’s partly the question the Mozilla Foundation , the 23-year-old accessibility-focused nonprofit behind the Firefox browser, is trying to answer with this year’s MozFest in Barcelona. Held this week, the Mozilla Festival is an annual global gathering of developers, policymakers, and tech builders focused on building a more human future for technology. This year, the festival is asking how to make the internet more human—or, in its words, how to “rewild” it. Fast Company spoke to Nabiha Syed, executive director of the Mozilla Foundation about this year’s festival, its themes, and why she believes nothing about the internet’s future is inevitable. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Tell me what rewilding means in this context of MozFest? We can acknowledge that we live in a moment where the Internet sometimes feels like a monoculture. There’s like six dudes in hoodies who are making decisions about what everybody should be consuming, the platforms we should be on, the things that shape the market. And what we know from nature is that monoculture works until it doesn’t. Until there’s a collapse in an ecosystem. So much of the open-source ideology that is core to Mozilla is about creating the structures for things to be wild and unpredictable and to go off in different directions and then later cross-pollinate. Last year’s theme for MozFest was unlearning: “Hey, we need to pause. What got us here isn’t necessarily gonna be what gets us to the next place?” Wilding is about saying, “Hey, what would it look like if we just let things bloom?” What if we had more people have more say over the way that we think the internet’s supposed to unfold and be? Describe what was the wild internet? And what is illustrative of a monoculture internet to you? I think about when I first learned how to code it was because I really wanted my MySpace to be amazing. I would view the source and make my page look like whatever I wanted it to look like. When I couldn’t quite get it that way, I’d go to GeoCities and make my own site in my own way. And there was freedom, interoperability, and contestability. Even in the blogosphere, the way that we spoke to one another felt like you were actually having conversations and not worrying about bot interjections. There was a feeling of possibility and not just predetermined ways of interacting like, “You can comment in this way,” or “You can engage in this way.” You got to create and build with the architecture as you wanted it. Every generation is always creative on any communications medium, but within the confines of a platform like Instagram. They can be innovative in how they use Finsta, or the way they shitpost, or the way they talk. But it’s still within the architecture that someone else has designed. What the early internet felt like to me, and to so many people who have nostalgia for that time, is that you could play with the rules of the game, and they were committed to interoperability, transparency, and being able to peer under the hood. Say more about what the consequences of that lack of interoperability, or the confined nature of our current platforms . To me, the big thing is that it creates what we call imagination deficit. articles.title: iPhone Duo Review: One Week Later
articles.content: It's been a week since the iPhone Duo was released, and MacRumors videographer Dan Barbera wanted to revisit his review since he's been able to use the Duo for a longer stretch of time. Subscribe to the MacRumors YouTube channel for more videos. You've probably seen images of iPhone Duos with a bright white line running across one side of the inner display. There is a defect affecting some users, but Apple says it's a problem limited to a small number of units. None of us at MacRumors have had a display crack, and we've seen some AI photos floating around, so it's hard to tell just how many people are actually having problems. iPhone Duos with the hinge issue that causes the display to crack seem to get damaged shortly after purchase, so if you've had an ‌iPhone Duo‌ for the last week and it's still fine, it's not likely to have this defect. The outer display is small, but Dan finds it useful for checking notifications, replying to messages, and scrolling through apps and websites. He unfolds it for multitasking or longer messages, and is a fan of using the ‌iPhone Duo‌ unfolded in portrait mode for watching videos and using an app at the same time. He finds the Touch ID fingerprint sensor easy to find, and says Apple Watch unlock is similar to Face ID . The cameras are just okay, and someone who zooms in a lot is probably going to miss having a telephoto lens. Battery life is between an iPhone 18 Pro and a Pro Max, and for most people, it's likely going to last a full day. Not all apps have been updated for the Duo layout yet, but it's getting better. There's an extension called Wider that extends the Safari window to the edges of the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s outer display, and it's a big improvement. We may see other accommodations in the coming months as developers and users get used to the new layout. Dan says the ‌iPhone Duo‌ is the most excited he's been about an iPhone in a long time, and he plans to keep using it even though he misses having a telephoto lens. Did you get an ‌iPhone Duo‌? What do you think now that you're a week into using it? Let us know in the comments below. articles.title: Q&A: Hey AI, who should I vote for this year?
articles.content: People are peppering artificial intelligence chatbots everyday with questions, but when it comes to politics and the looming 2026 U.S. midterm elections, what role are AI platforms playing? Could an AI chatbot sway a voter to switch parties or re-examine their political beliefs? MIT researchers have built a new dashboard, called the LLM Election Observatory , to examine, in real-time, how popular AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 midterm elections. The team behind the dashboard — led by Professor Adam Berinsky , Assistant Professor Chara Podimata , and Professor Charles Stewart III — has extensive experience studying voting and election administration, AI and misinformation, and how AI systems are impacting human decision making. In an effort to better understand how AI is shaping the election, they designed the dashboard to simulate how individuals across the country communicate with chatbots. The team tracks how different AI systems respond to the same fixed set of questions on a range of topics, including election certification, hot-button issues, result predictions, news coverage, and more. Every few days, the LLM Election Observatory team runs the questions through the chatbots again, monitoring how their responses vary as the election gets closer depending on user location, political party affiliation, identity and other factors. The goal of this work is not to merely understand how AI systems spread information, but also better comprehend how they are shaping political discourse and voter understanding of political issues across the country. MIT News chatted with Podimata, the Class of 1942 Career Development Professor, an assistant professor of operations research and statistics in the MIT Sloan School of Management, and a member of the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems; and Berinsky, the Mitsui Professor and a professor in the Department of Political Science, about their work with the LLM Election Observatory, how AI could impact the midterms, and what voters should keep in mind when they interact with chatbots. Q : What was the inspiration for this project and what are you hoping to learn through the LLM Election Observatory? Podimata : People are increasingly using AI chatbots to find and make sense of political and election-related information. That makes it important to understand what information these systems actually provide, not just at one moment in time but throughout an election cycle. This is particularly challenging because the models themselves are continually getting updates, the political information inputs available to them are themselves changing, and their answers can depend on how a user asks a question or what information the user provides about themselves. One basic problem is that we currently do not have a good historical record of this information environment. If an AI system gives a particular answer about an election today and gives a different answer several weeks later, it can be very difficult to reconstruct after the fact what voters would have seen at each point in time. One important goal of our project is simply to systematically document that environment as it develops and make the resulting data available to other researchers and to the public. Ultimately, factual accuracy is only the first frontier. We absolutely need to understand whether chatbots provide accurate political information, but we also need to pay just as much attention to the subtler ways in which they may shape people’s understanding of political issues. Differences in framing, emphasis, uncertainty, and cited sources can matter enormously, even in the absence of outright misinformation. Q : Professor Podimata, you studied how LLMs shaped political discourse and information during the 2024 election. What were the main takeaways of that research and how did those findings inform this new project? Podimata : The LLM Election Observatory builds on my previous work during the 2024…

articles.title: MacBook Pro With Touch Display: 15 More Details Revealed
articles.content: Apple on Wednesday unveiled new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with touch-enabled OLED displays , and more details about them continue to be shared by tech reporters who were invited to Apple's hands-on experience in Los Angeles. Nicolas Lellouche of the French website Numerama shared 15 details about the new MacBook Pro models in an article and a social media post . Some of this information has already surfaced, but he provided a useful summary: Apple said the keyboard and trackpad remain the primary input methods, with touch input available as an additional option for those who want it. Apple said there is now a generation of young creators who grew up using touchscreens, so it felt the timing was right to bring the functionality to the Mac. Apple said music creators prefer touch over trackpads for controlling virtual instruments. "Traffic light" controls in the top-left corner of macOS windows expand when pressed. Items in a list become more spaced out when touched. A swipe up from the bottom of the screen brings up the Dock. A swipe down from the top of the screen brings up Spotlight/Siri AI. A long press is equivalent to a right click. Holding a window and quickly moving it left or right triggers Split View. If you close your Mac while your finger is touching the display, touch input is temporarily deactivated to prevent accidental touches. The camera is stabilized so it does not shake on video calls when you touch the screen. You cannot wake the MacBook Pro by touching the screen. Multi-touch supports up to 10 fingers at the same time. No word yet on toes (kidding). Live Activities from iPhone apps can appear in the Dynamic Island. There are settings that allow you to turn off touch input and the illuminated Apple logo on the MacBook Pro's lid. The new MacBook Pro models can be pre-ordered now and launch Friday, November 6. articles.title: I still think the Mac mini M4 is 'the best small form factor PC in the world' — and it’s $150 off at Best Buy
articles.content: The Apple Mac mini M6 may be catching all the headlines right now, but I still think for most people looking for a stylish and powerful mini PC, the Mac mini M4 is the optimal choice. It might lack the extra oomph of the M6, but for daily office tasks and content creation, it's way better value. Case in point. The Apple Mac mini M4 is currently $650 (was $799) at Best Buy . If you want a fast, compact desktop for work, photo editing, or everyday use, and you already own a monitor and keyboard, the Mac mini M4 is the best-value Mac you can buy. Meanwhile, Best Buy has the Mac mini M6 for $799 (was $899) . • Best for: Professionals and creators upgrading an older Mac or Windows mini PC to a powerful, near-silent desktop without paying M6 prices. . • Why we like it: We scored this machine 5 stars in our review, and wondered if it might actually be the best Mac ever. For most people, it will be. Apple’s speedy M4 chip, 16GB of unified memory for smooth multitasking and Apple Intelligence, a tiny five-inch-square design, and handy front-facing USB-C ports and a headphone jack. Mac mini M4: was $799 now $649 A compact desktop with Apple’s M4 chip, 16GB of unified memory, and a 256GB SSD, with front USB-C ports and a headphone jack, plus Thunderbolt, HDMI, and Ethernet on the back. It supports Apple Intelligence and comes in silver. View Deal Why we recommend it In our Mac mini M4 review , our expert Matt awarded it an Editor’s Choice badge and full marks for value, praising its strong performance, much smaller design, and convenient front ports. He called it the cheapest way into the Mac ecosystem, though he noted it struggles with modern games and that its power button sits awkwardly on the underside. Our review unit had a 512GB SSD rather than this model’s 256GB, but it used the same M4 chip and 16GB of memory. Price Context & Historical Value Apple raised the Mac mini’s starting price to $799 earlier this year as memory costs surged, so this $150 discount is measured against Apple’s real current price rather than an inflated list price. It’s still more than the $599 the M4 Mac mini launched at, and well above the sub-$500 deals we saw before the price hike. Given today’s pricing, though, $649 is a strong deal and a good time to buy. For comparison, the Mac mini M6 is currently down to $799 at Best Buy . For some workloads, it may be better. For general office tasks, the M4 is still worth considering for its value. Should you buy it? ✅ Buy the Apple Mac mini M4 if... you want an affordable, powerful Mac desktop, you already have a monitor, keyboard, and mouse, or you want a near-silent machine for work, photo editing, or music production. ❌ Skip the Apple Mac mini M4 if... you need lots of local storage, since 256GB fills quickly; you want to play the latest PC games; or you don’t already own a monitor and accessories, which add to the total cost. See all Apple deals at Best Buy .

articles.title: The Google Nest Wifi Pro is the simplest Wi-Fi 6E mesh router I’d set up for non-techy family members — and it’s half price at Best Buy
articles.content: I don't know about you, but I'm sort of the gadget-man of the family. The tech-head. The makeshift IT consultant that gets called upon whenever there's an issue with technology. If you fall into the same category (or you never want to call on your family IT support again), I'd definitely recommend checking out the Google Nest Wifi Pro 6e Wi-Fi mesh router for $100 (was $200) at Best Buy . The half-price deal makes it incredibly tempting. It's ridiculously simple to set up and manage, making it the ideal no-fuss mesh router pick if you or your family need better connections while working from home. If your home Wi-Fi is spotty and you don’t want to wrestle with complicated router settings, Nest Wifi Pro delivers fast, reliable coverage with minimal setup. • Best for: home workers and families in small to midsize homes needing fast, easy-to-manage Wi-Fi with the option to add more units later. • Why we like it: tri-band Wi-Fi 6E with a 6GHz band for less congestion, up to 2,200 square feet of coverage from one unit, effortless setup through the Google Home app, and support for adding more units to build a mesh. Nest WiFi Pro: was $199 now $99 A single tri-band Wi-Fi 6E (AXE5400) mesh router covering 2.4GHz, 5GHz, and 6GHz bands, with up to 2,200 square feet of coverage, support for up to 100 connected devices, WPA3 security, parental controls, and two Gigabit Ethernet ports. It’s managed through the Google Home app and also works as a Thread border router and Matter controller for smart home devices. Sold by Best Buy. View Deal Why We Recommend It Google built the Nest Wifi Pro for people who want Wi-Fi to simply work, and its app-based setup and automatic updates make it one of the least intimidating routers to own. We haven’t reviewed the Nest Wifi Pro, so this pick rests on Google’s track record with mesh networking and the router’s specs. Its 6GHz band is a real plus if you have newer phones and laptops that support Wi-Fi 6E, since it’s far less crowded than the older bands. Price Context & Historical Value Half off its $199.99 launch price is a strong deal, and $99.99 puts a Wi-Fi 6E mesh router within reach of almost any budget. Keep in mind that it launched in 2022, so it lacks the newer Wi-Fi 7 standard and multi-gig Ethernet found on pricier routers. For most homes with internet plans under 1Gbps, though, it’s a great buy at this price. Should you buy it? ✅ Buy the Google Nest Wifi Pro if... you want fast Wi-Fi that’s easy to set up and manage, your home is under about 2,200 square feet or you plan to add more units, or you use Google Home and want a router that doubles as a smart home hub. ❌ Skip the Google Nest Wifi Pro if... you want Wi-Fi 7 or multi-gig Ethernet ports for a very fast internet plan, you need lots of wired ports, or you already own older Google Wifi or Nest Wifi units, which can’t join a Nest Wifi Pro mesh. See more router deals at Best Buy .

articles.title: Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch
articles.content: Powerlattice founders, from left: Gang Ren, Peng Zou, and Sujith Dermal. (Powerlattice / Walden Kirsch Photo) Powerlattice , a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday. The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment. AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling. “AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A. Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators. CEO Peng Zou , Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan. Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon. In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors. “Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser

articles.title: The Geekom Air12 Lite is the kind of tiny, low-cost PC I’d set up for basic browsing and email — and it’s $269 at Best Buy
articles.content: When it comes to our testing, Geekom has a strong track record in mini PCs. The range runs from high-performance machines for content creation and heavy workloads to compact machines built for general office duty, browsing, streaming, and other undemanding tasks. The Geekom Air12 Lite, currently $269 (was $599) at Best Buy , falls into the latter camp. If you need a small, cheap PC for a kitchen counter, a kid’s homework desk, or a living room TV, the Air12 Lite covers the basics without taking up any space. • Best for: anyone who needs a simple, compact computer for web browsing, email, documents, and streaming video. • Why we like it: a tiny, quiet design, a quad-core Intel N95 processor that handles everyday tasks, a 256GB SSD, and Windows 11 Pro preinstalled. • What you need to know: The Intel N95 is a low-power chip that’s built for browsing, email, office documents, and streaming, but it will feel sluggish with lots of tabs open or more demanding software. Air12 Lite: was $599 now $269 A compact mini PC with a quad-core, four-thread Intel Processor N95 boosting to 3.4GHz, integrated Intel UHD graphics, 8GB of DDR4 memory, a 256GB SSD, and Windows 11 Pro. Sold and shipped by Geekom through Best Buy’s marketplace. View Deal Why we recommend it Geekom has built a solid reputation for well-made mini PCs, and the Air12 Lite is its entry-level model, designed for light everyday tasks rather than heavy workloads. We haven’t tested it ourselves, so this pick rests on Geekom’s track record and the specs. We have, however, tested the improved Air12, which features DDR5 RAM and Wi-Fi 6 connectivity. We scored that machine 4 stars in our review , and for general office tasks, expect performance to be about the same. Price Context & Historical Value Ignore the $599 comparison price, since that’s far more than an N95 mini PC with 8GB of RAM has ever been worth, and budget machines with this chip have typically sold for well under $300. Rising memory prices have pushed up the cost of mini PCs this year, so $269 is a reasonable price today rather than a steal. Buy it if you need a basic PC now, but don’t expect much more than browsing and email from it. Should you buy it? ✅ Buy the Geekom Air12 Lite if... you need an inexpensive, compact PC for browsing, email, documents, and streaming, you want Windows 11 Pro preinstalled, or you’re setting up a simple machine for a family member. ❌ Skip the Geekom Air12 Lite if... you plan to multitask heavily or run demanding apps, since 8GB of RAM and the N95 chip will feel limited; you want to play games; or you’d rather spend a bit more for a mini PC with a faster processor. articles.title: Google’s satellite AI server transmits its first response to Earth
articles.content: Google's AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post on Friday, Google says it successfully booted up the satellite's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), allowing the on-board Gemma 4 model to follow through on a prompt to create a haiku about being in space: Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨ Google says it tried out other space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts as well. The test is part of Google's Project Suncatcher, an experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers in space. articles.title: We asked which Googlebook you’d buy and many said they’d pass
articles.content: A little over a month ago, we got our first look at Google’s Android-derived line of Googlebooks . Googlebooks are designed to let users seamlessly switch between their phones and laptops to create a true Android ecosystem. It’s a little too early to tell if they’ll succeed, but we wanted to know if they won you over yet. So we asked you which one of the five you would buy (or if you even want one at all) in a poll. The Lenovo Googlebook 15 came out on top with 19% of the vote. It has a 15.3-inch display and comes in at 2.84 pounds, making it the biggest of the group. With Lenovo behind it, it holds the promise of being a reliable, if pricey workhorse, starting at $1,299.

At this price, it’s an easy recommendation for anyone who wants a quality mesh chair without spending $300 or more. Should you buy it? ✅ Buy the Boulies EP200 if... you want a comfortable, breathable mesh chair for long workdays, you need adjustable lumbar support and a headrest, or you’re after quality ergonomics without a premium price. ❌ Skip the Boulies EP200 if... you need the fine-tuned adjustability of a high-end ergonomic chair, or you prefer a padded backrest to mesh. articles.title: Rare meteorite from Mars gives us a view into its ancient crust
articles.content: Crater counts tell us that most of the Martian surface is more than 3 billion years old, but pieces of Mars we have on Earth tell a different story. The three main classes of Martian meteorites—shergottites, nakhlites, and chassignites—are all 2.4 billion years old or younger. Until now, only two genuinely ancient Martian meteorites were known: Allan Hills 84001, found in Antarctica, and a jumbled rock from northwest Africa nicknamed Black Beauty. Now we have a third one. A team led by Yang Liu, a planetary scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, has shown that a Martian meteorite called Teghaza 001, found in the Sahara Desert in Mali in 2022, formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. “It's very old and similar to some of the oldest rocks on Earth,” Liu says. A filtered collection “We don't fully understand why old Martian rocks are so rare on Earth," Liu said. Part of the answer may lie in how a piece of Mars gets here. It takes a large impact to launch a rock off the planet, and not every rock can survive that. “If the impact hits into loose powder, it may not get cemented to become a rock and fly off Mars' gravity,” Liu said. “So the natural impact already acts as a filter. Weak rocks do not make it off Mars.” Read full article Comments
articles.author: Jacek Krywko

articles.title: GM Reaches $220 Million Settlement Over Selling Drivers' Private Data
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: General Motors will pay $220 million to 36 states to settle allegations that it illegally sold private driving behavior and location information to data brokers. As part of the settlement, GM must get drivers' express consent before it collects or shares their driving and location data -- terms that are in line with separate agreements it previously reached with California and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). This settlement does contain a new requirement that GM must have a third party assess the automaker's compliance with the privacy program it has put in place. The agreement announced Thursday settles a lawsuit brought by a coalition of attorneys general from 36 states that alleged GM had sold the information to data brokers, which in turn then sold it to insurance providers. "This agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we've taken to strengthen our privacy practices," GM said in an emailed statement. "Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it's protected, and the choices customers have about what they share." The settlement comes more than two years after a New York Times report showed how GM and OnStar collected, used, and sold drivers' precise geolocation data and driving behavior to third parties, including data brokers LexisNexis and Verisk. The data was collected through GM's Smart Driver program, a free feature contained within its connected car apps that tracked and rated driving behaviors and seat belt use. Data brokers sold this information to insurance providers, which could affect customers' rates, the NYT reported at the time. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Meet TokenEconomizer: Microsoft’s Plugin That Cuts Coding Agent Costs by Up to 30.9%
articles.content: A team of researchers from Microsoft Research and UC Berkeley have released TokenEconomizer , an open-source cost controller for coding agents. TokenEconomizer is a plugin that learns from past sessions in a repository to cut waste in later ones. It works with Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI and Pi. It does not touch model weights or agent code. On 277 SWE-Bench tasks, it lowered mean cost by 18.4% to 30.9% across 5 agent-model settings. TL;DR Package: A standard-library Python package and agent plugins, with 3 switchable mechanisms. Runs on: Any machine running Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI or Pi with Python 3.10+. No GPU and no API key of its own. Performance: 18.4% to 30.9% lower mean SWE-Bench cost, and cheaper in all 30 repository-setting cells. Best: 30.9% lower cost on Claude Code with Opus 4.8 (33.2% when combined with RTK). Worst: Only 6.4% to 9.3% savings on ReposVul audits; Pass@1 drops 1.0 point on Opus 4.8. Why do coding agents waste tokens? Every agent turn re-bills the system prompt, every loaded tool schema and the full history. The research team profiled 60 SWE-Bench tasks across 6 repositories using Claude Code with Opus 4.8. They found 3 recurring sources of waste: Repeated discovery: once 5 tasks precede the current one, 30% of tool calls repeat an earlier action. Unused tools: 23 tool schemas load every turn. 16 are never called, and 3 cover 98% of calls. Failure loops: 10 failed runs were 17% of tasks but 32% of total spend. They also tested 3 fixed open-source strategies: RTK , Serena and Aider’s RepoMap . None was cheaper everywhere. All 3 cut cost on Django and raised it on SymPy. How does TokenEconomizer work? TokenEconomizer is an external controller that treats the agent as a black box. It keeps a state per repository, built from completed traces. Before each task, it sets 3 policies through the prompt, the tool settings and the event stream. 1. Micro-skills An LLM proposer turns trace digests into 1-line facts, such as the working test command. Each fact carries regex detectors that check later traces without a model call. A fact enters the prompt after 3 confirmations on tasks with non-overlapping edited files. Its need rate must also stay at or above 0.4. One contradiction counts as 5 confirmations, so wrong facts retire quickly. 2. Tool pruning Shell, read, write and edit tools are always kept. Other tools are masked after 3 consecutive unused tasks, or when an LLM judge marks them irrelevant. The full catalog returns every 5 tasks for a re-audit. On Django with Claude Code, the first request on task 2 fell from 43,351 to 16,295 prompt tokens. 3. Failure-loop intervention The controller learns a turn budget: 1.25 times the 90th percentile of successful run lengths. Cheap rule checks flag repeated failures or dense errors. An LLM judge then decides if the agent is stuck, at 0.7 confidence or higher. A stuck agent gets 1 redirect, then a stop if the loop recurs. What do the SWE-Bench results show? Setting Cost vs default Pass@1 default Pass@1 TokenEconomizer Claude Code + Sonnet 5 -23.6% 74.7 76.0 Claude Code + Opus 4.8 -30.9% 74.0 73.0 Codex + GPT-5.6 Terra -24.7% 73.8 74.7 Codex + GPT-5.6 Sol -26.1% 80.1 81.7 Copilot CLI + Sonnet 5 -18.4% 75.0 77.6 Source: arXiv 2610.22732 , Table 1. Costs include all controller calls. 3 seeds per setting. Pass@1 improved in 4 of 5 settings. Lower reasoning effort saved cost but cut Pass@1 by 1.8 to 10.3 points. RTK alone raised cost in 12 of 30 repository-setting cells, and RepoMap in 15. Savings build over time. Most repositories cost more at first, but all were cheaper by the sixth task. Alone on Claude Code, tool pruning saved 13.2% to 17.7%, micro-skills 11.8% to 14.3%, and the loop guard 5.4% to 7.1%. Results also held outside SWE-Bench. Costs fell 16.0% to 21.2% on Web-Bench and 16.5% to 19.6% on CredData. ReposVul saw only 6.4% to 9.3%, because shorter runs leave less to remove. How does it compare with other token-saving tools?
