articles.title: Binance Suffers Biggest Crypto Hack In History With $6.3 Billion Affected [UPDATE]
articles.content: UPDATE 10/30/26: Binance has temporarily suspended customer withdrawals after suffering what investigators say is the biggest crypto hack in history. According to Binance CEO Yi He, the company estimates roughly $6.3 billion in funds were impacted, with roughly $3 billion in assets frozen on-chain so far. Rest assured, "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss," said co-CEO Richard Teng in a LinkedIn post. "This was a complex attack," said Teng. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers, making it more difficult for us to trace." From a report: Teng said the incident was not carried out by one person. While the initial investigation indicated the involvement of a compromised laptop, further digging revealed additional points of breach. [...] Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Elliptic have linked the theft to North Korean hackers, with TRM attributing it "with high confidence" to a group known as TraderTraitor, the same group responsible for last year's Bybit hack. Elliptic estimated Friday that about 44% of the stolen assets have been frozen, with stablecoins accounting for nearly all of those funds. The firm estimated that attackers still controlled over $3 billion in crypto that token issuers cannot directly freeze. The hackers appear to have compromised Binance's wallet-signing infrastructure, allowing them to authorize transactions that drained billions of dollars in cryptocurrency across multiple blockchains, according to the firms. Binance, in its preliminary stage, has conducted an investigation into the hack, which suggests the incident may have begun with a compromised engineer's laptop. The exchange added that it has found no evidence that wallet passwords were leaked. Below is the original story from yesterday, Oct. 29th. Binance is investigating a potential hack after more than $2 billion in crypto was drained from one of its wallets into a new external account, with Blockaid estimating nearly $3.3 billion was moved. "Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating," said Binance on X. "User funds are safe," said Binance founder CZ. "It does look like a hack on Binance. Appreciate the quick freeze from Tether (~$971m) and Circle (~$823m). I don't manage Binance anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered." At around the same time, crypto-based prediction market Polymarket reported its own security incident that wiped out around $2.7 million in user funds. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: At launch, there were more iPhone Duo in stores than online
articles.content: Apple chose to have perhaps four times more iPhone Duo stock at retail than for sale online on launch day, and even so, most went home empty-handed. Apple arranged its limited iPhone Duo stock so that most went to Apple Stores instead of to online pre-orders. Apple described demand for the iPhone Duo as being "extraordinary," and manufacturer Foxconn has talked about using its international facilities to produce more. Certainly the pre-order stock sold out instantaneously , although a new report suggests there was a reason for that. According to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman, Apple elected to route the greater number of iPhone Duo units to Apple Stores instead of keeping them for online pre-orders. Citing people said to be close to Apple's logistics planning, he says on his " Power On " podcast that as much as 80% of the stock was reserved for the stores. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
articles.content: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens. Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI. Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on. The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies. “As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.” Terabits a Second, Processed in Flight Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold. At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI , a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther , a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS . Nexus , a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. The system can handle 2.4 terabits per second on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with inference running on premises, next to the instrument. Put together, the system enables an agent to steer a telescope’s antennae, calibrate and focus the instrument for a clean signal, catch and fix data errors and plot the result. Agents compress what would take humans weeks or years into hours. Science Fact, Not Fiction The pipeline has already proven itself, achieving the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar — a rapidly spinning stellar remnant that pulses like a cosmic lighthouse — in the Crab Nebula. Next, the team is evaluating open models including NVIDIA Nemotron for cases where data locality and turnaround matter most and for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the moon. Learn more about NVIDIA AI for science .
articles.author: Chris Porter

articles.title: The Tragedy of Losing Your Wikipedia Page
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes an excerpt from a Wired article that explores the often-contentious process of nominating pages for deletion when their subjects fail to meet the encyclopedia's notability standards: What do you need to know -- need to know -- about Xavier Trudeau? The eldest son of former Canadian prime minister Justin, the teenage Trudeau has recently begun performing R&B under the mononym Xav. But, with all due respect to Xav, do those facts make him a person of note? Should you expect to be able to read about him on Wikipedia? What about Evanescence guitarist Tim McCord, or 2012 Yachtmaster of the Year Rainer Holtorff? All three have had a biography on Wikipedia; all three of those biographies were considered for deletion this year on the grounds that the subjects were not notable enough to warrant a biography at all. Every day, dozens, sometimes hundreds, of Wikipedia biographies -- of child actors turned LA realtors, retired ambassadors, soccer players who have played less than 10 minutes of professional soccer -- are purged from the world's free encyclopedia. It's not as though Wikipedia, which hosts over 7 million articles in the English language, doesn't have the space. But Wikipedia has only so many volunteers to monitor its contents. To this day, Wikipedia editors are discovering hoaxes that have gone undetected for decades. The time it takes to verify the release dates of Xav's three singles is better spent -- the logic goes -- by asking whether the American Civil War officer Nathaniel Lyon really drank mustard during battle, as was claimed in his Wikipedia biography for 17 years. Wikipedia removed the mustard claim, not because it was proven wrong, but because there was no reliable evidence for it. "We're not really looking for what's true," Britta Gustafson, who has been editing Wikipedia since 2001, told me. "We're looking for what's verifiable." Wikipedia editors do not themselves decide that a person is not notable, only that there is a lack of reliable evidence to support the claim... Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Polymarket trading paused over a security issue involving this third-party UK provider
articles.content: Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international platform Thursday because of a security incident that compromised a third-party provider, the company said. Trading was paused for about an hour and resumed Thursday afternoon. The company has promised to fully reimburse any affected traders. The prediction market platform said it halted trading “out of an abundance of caution” after identifying and fixing the issue affecting its international platform. “We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders,” the company posted on X once trading had resumed. Polymarket said it referred the incident to a law enforcement agency in the United Kingdom. Reports have linked the source of the incident to DebugBear, a UK-based company offering website performance monitoring tools. DebugBear’s own website was unavailable Thursday afternoon and the company posted on X that it was “impacted by an ongoing security incident.” It also advised clients who were using one of its products to remove the embed code from their websites. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It was not immediately clear to what extent traders using the popular prediction market platform were impacted, or the breadth of the impact. The company said anyone who was impacted “will be made whole.” —Kaitlyn Huamani, AP Technology Writer

articles.title: GPT-6.1 Terra vs. GPT-6 Astra: One sacrifices accuracy for lower cost and higher speed at high effort
articles.content: OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra on October 26, marketing it as a cheap, fast model for high-volume everyday work, priced at a tenth of its GPT-6 Astra flagship. As the mid-priced model in its GPT-6 family , OpenAI lists Terra at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, a mere tenth of Astra’s $10 and $50. The AI giant also reports that Terra completes tasks more than three times faster than Astra in its Agents’ Last Exam benchmark. Those computer-use results are not directly comparable to the three tests below. Early benchmarks showed some limitations, alongside gains. Plotly reported that Terra caught three of five planted patterns in its analytics test and passed 40 of 43 questions overall. Artificial Analysis found that it guessed on 38% of questions it couldn’t answer instead of saying so, down from 88% for GPT-5.6 Terra in the same benchmark. DualEntry’s accounting benchmark put its accuracy at 78.2%. In this AI arms race, each launch needs to be marketed as the best; otherwise, it risks being ignored. This can create a confusing experience for users, especially when reality doesn’t quite match the promise. I compared Terra with Astra on three synthetic tasks to see how their speed, estimated token costs, and accuracy differed. This is a separate test of those trade-offs, not a replication of OpenAI’s computer-use benchmark. The tests I ran the final version of each test once per model through OpenAI’s API with reasoning effort set to high. I didn’t set an output-token cap, though the models still have built-in output limits. I graded each test against keys I built and verified, after developing three versions of each test. These are single-run results on synthetic tasks, not estimates of repeatability or performance across all workloads. Matching the effort setting does not impose the same reasoning-token budget on both models. Both models returned the same score on easy and medium-difficulty tests. To test the real soft spots, after the same results returned a third time, I ran hard tests against a weaker model, GPT-5 Mini, until Mini’s score was very low. Here is the final iteration of the tests. These are the tests detailed in the remainder of this article. In the usage figures below, “out” includes reasoning tokens; the parenthetical reasoning count is a subset, not an additional charge. Costs are estimates calculated from the reported tokens at standard uncached input and output rates, excluding any tool charges or billing adjustments. They are not verified invoice totals. SQL reasoning – I built a fake database of 500 software builds and asked each model 25 questions about it. Some builds were deleted, some were retries, costs are in three currencies, and a few questions depend on time zones. Two of the questions can’t be answered from the data. Data validation – I gave each model a spreadsheet of 4,950 fake customer records and 19 rules they’re supposed to follow. Some rules only make sense across the whole file, like no more than three customers at one postal code and no referral loops; forty records break a rule, and 10 look wrong but are actually fine. Incident log triage – I wrote about 7,000 lines of logs from a fake outage across more than 20 services. I planted errors like drifting clocks, error messages blaming the wrong service, and unrelated changes sending alerts before the one that actually caused the outage. SQL reasoning This test showed the widest split between the two models. Astra scored 48/50 and Terra 26/50. Each of the 25 questions was worth two points, for a total of 50. An answer had to be exactly right to earn the two points, so a close answer earned zero. Unanswered questions also earned zero points. For the questions that can’t be answered from the data, the correct answer was to identify that. On every other question, a model that didn’t give an answer earned zero. Terra processed all 500 rows and handled soft deletes, retries, and three currencies. Its one miss was…

articles.title: Russia Places Apple on State Surveillance Registry
articles.content: Apple faces Russian data retention and disclosure requirements after being added to the country's state surveillance registry, Bloomberg reports. Russia's communications regulator, Roskomnadzor, listed Apple and Microsoft on October 2 as "organizers of information dissemination," a classification that carries obligations to preserve communications and make data available to Russian security agencies. Those obligations cover correspondence and messages containing audio or video. Companies must also keep information identifying users and recording the transmission of their communications within Russia for three years. Businesses that fail to meet the requirements risk fines and, ultimately, restrictions on their services. Apple and Microsoft join other services on the registry, including WhatsApp, Telegram, and Snapchat. Google and its Meet video calling service were listed in January. The designation follows Russia's December 2025 block on FaceTime . Roskomnadzor justified that restriction by alleging the service was being used to facilitate terrorism, recruitment, and fraud. Russia had already restricted calling through WhatsApp and Telegram and blocked Signal and Viber. Apple suspended sales in Russia in March 2022 following the invasion of Ukraine, in addition to stopping exports into its Russian sales channel and limiting Apple Pay . articles.title: AlpineBSD announced – an AI-free FOSS OS
articles.content: Just days after Daemonarchy, there's another new OS in the BSD family – and one that is heading determinedly in almost the opposite direction. AlpineBSD is so new that it barely exists yet. There are no installation media available, though it's possible to manually bootstrap an installation . What AlpineBSD does already have is an AI policy, and the plan is to avoid "the output of generative AI models (e.g. LLMs)" as far as possible: "Any software whose code, documentation, binaries, or other assets include, in any part, the output of a generative AI tool such as an LLM, is considered 'tainted' for our purposes." The core idea is to combine the kernel of NetBSD with "a userspace inspired by Alpine Linux and the objective of making it possible to use as little AI-generated software as possible." Back in 2024 , the NetBSD project made its position on AI plain. Its commit guidelines say that "code generated by a Large Language Model […] is presumed to be tainted code." Back in July, Linus Torvalds stated that "Linux is not one of those anti-AI projects ". Since then, NetBSD has seen a spike in donations and interest . For someone mainly used to Linux, trying to install NetBSD is a little like hopping in a time machine to 30 years ago, and we speak from personal experience of Linux in the mid-1990s. As we mentioned when Slackware turned 30 a few years ago, back in 1996, this vulture tried Slackware 3.0 on his own hardware, and we never did manage to install it. We tried NetBSD 11 a couple of months ago , and despite considerable help from the folks on the NetBSD-users mailing list, we failed to get the CDE desktop to start. As an example, installing software on NetBSD is not the easy, comfortable task it is on Linux. It does have a package manager for handling binary packages: it's called pkgin , but as the NetBSD FAQ mentions , it's an optional extra. You must manually tick a box in the setup program to install pkgin with the rest of the OS, and when we tried NetBSD 9.3 four years ago , we didn't know that, overlooked that checkbox, and had to find a way to add pkgin later. (It is quite tricky to install a package manager when you don't have a package manager to install it with.) This time around, we discovered that pkgin sometimes doesn't complete the installation process for you – it just leaves a text file in a destination directory somewhere, and you're expected to know that, go there, read it, and do any further steps yourself. The NetBSD community has been quietly going its own way since 1993. It has its own ideas about what is normal, and its users expect that. Some folks on the mailing list told us that they never use binary packages anyway – they compile what they need from source code. AlpineBSD's ports repository and source code are hosted on Sourcehut, under the account of sircmpwn , better known as Drew DeVault . We have quoted DeVault a few times over the years: we've often found that his views align with our own in various ways… such as about t he best laptops ever made , and on simplicity in Linux distro design , or even on dot-com billionaires at FOSDEM . Alpine's tools are quite well-suited to being adapted to other systems. We have previously mentioned the use of its packaging tool, APK, in the GNU-free Chimera Linux , which uses much of the FreeBSD userland, and also in Adélie Linux . We will follow AlpineBSD with interest. There's strong appeal in the plan of combining perhaps the best-known, longest-established AI-free Unix-like kernel with the user-facing parts of pretty much the smallest and cleanest Linux distro there is. The AI advocates often warn LLM skeptics that they risk being left behind. Well, here's an OS for those who don't want to surf the AI wave. ®

articles.title: Creating Custom (Code-Based) Agent Evaluators in Microsoft Foundry with Python
articles.content: AGENTIC AI Build, register, and debug an evaluator using the Foundry SDK. Plus some common runtime errors discussed. Introduction Microsoft Foundry has several built-in evaluators for measuring things such as intent resolution, task adherence, groundedness, and tool-call accuracy. These are a very useful starting point to evaluate an agent because we can add them to an evaluation run without writing the scoring logic ourselves. The setup is also super simple, with the option to create them on Foundry Playground or via SDK. But what happens when the quality check is specific to our application or agent? Or the agent caters to judgment tasks, like how well did it respond to a customer complaint? For instance, I have a fact-checker agent that searches the web and returns the sources used to verify a claim. In addition to checking whether the agent understood the task (i.e. intent_resolution), I want to ask a more application-specific question: Did the agent return enough sources for the input claim and were these sources recent enough? As of date, there is no built-in evaluator called source_recency, so I created a custom code-based evaluator for it. The scoring logic (between 0 and 1) is straightforward: 0 if returned sources were not dated (i.e., no published or updated date available) 0.5 if at least one of the returned sources was dated and fulfilled recency requirements 1 if all the returned sources were dated and fulfilled recency requirements In the rest of the article, we will learn how to (a) write this custom evaluator, (b) register it in Foundry so anyone on your team can call it as easily as the built-in evaluators, and (c) run an eval dataset against it. Let’s begin! What are custom code-based evaluators? A code-based evaluator is a deterministic Python function that Foundry runs for every item in the evaluation dataset. It is useful when the scoring rule can be expressed without asking another LLM to judge the response. Some examples include: checking whether a response is valid JSON; verifying that mandatory fields are present; measuring response length; detecting whether citations were returned; confirming that enough sources meet a date threshold; or validating an application-specific output format. Apart from code-based evaluators, we can also create prompt-based evaluators . Every code-based evaluator must expose a grade function with this shape: def grade(sample: dict, item: dict) -> float: ... It takes only two inputs — sample which is the output from the agent and item which is each row in the eval dataset. The function returns a single float between 0.0 and 1.0, where a higher value is better. Note: Code-based evaluators are best suited to deterministic rules. If the requirement is subjective — for example, “Does this response sound empathetic?” — a prompt-based evaluator is usually a better fit. Easiest mental mapping is, if you need to use LLM-as-a-judge i.e. an LLM will score an agent output for qualities like politeness, rudeness, sentiment, etc. then use prompt-based evaluator. Prerequisites For this example, I am using: Python 3.10 or above; azure-ai-projects==2.8.0; azure-identity; python-dotenv; and an existing Microsoft Foundry project containing an agent and a model deployment. Install the packages: pip install azure-ai-projects==2.8.0 pip install azure-identity pip install python-dotenv Create a .env file containing the project endpoint and the deployment used by the evaluation service: AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT="https://<account>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project>" JUDGE_MODEL_DEPLOYMENT="gpt-4o-mini" Note: The evaluator catalog and some evaluation APIs are still preview features. The exact API surface can change between SDK versions, so pinning the version is helpful when you want the same code to behave consistently across environments. articles.title: How to Ship Safely With Feature Flags: OpenFeature, Gradual Rollouts and Kill Switches
articles.content: A Hands-On TypeScript Guide to Decoupling Deploys From Releases, With Tested Code for Targeting, Telemetry and Flag Cleanup Photo by Jeroen Overschie on Unsplash Most production incidents do not start with a bad idea. They start with a good change that reached every user at the same moment. A new checkout flow, a rewritten search query or a migration to a new payment provider can pass every test and still fail under real traffic, and when it does, the only lever many teams have is a rollback that takes 20 minutes and another deploy. Feature flags fix that by separating two things we usually treat as one: deploying code and releasing behaviour. The catch is that flags are easy to add and hard to live with. Every flag is a branch in production that nobody tests in every combination, a hidden configuration dependency and, if it is never removed, a piece of permanent debt. Teams also tend to lock themselves into one vendor SDK that ends up sprinkled through hundreds of files. In this post we will build a small but realistic setup in TypeScript with OpenFeature, the vendor-neutral flag API, and flagd as the flag engine: percentage rollouts, user targeting, a kill switch, evaluation telemetry and an automated check that stops flags from living forever. Every code sample was run against @openfeature/server-sdk 1.23.0 and @openfeature/flagd-provider 0.18.0. The Problem Without flags, a release is binary. The moment a deploy finishes, 100% of users get the new code. If something goes wrong, you roll back the whole deploy, including any unrelated fixes that shipped with it. That pushes teams towards long-lived branches, big releases and release-day nerves. The opposite failure is just as real. The most famous feature flag accident is the Knight Capital incident of August 1, 2012. According to the SEC order , Knight reused an old flag to switch on new trading code, but one of its eight servers never received the new deploy. On that server the flag woke up dormant code from years earlier, which sent more than 4 million executions into the market in about 45 minutes and cost the firm over $460 million. The lessons are still relevant: never repurpose a flag, remove dead code behind old flags, and make sure every instance evaluates flags the same way. So we want three things at once: the ability to release gradually and turn things off instantly, a consistent evaluation model across services, and a process that keeps the number of flags under control. Core Concepts Pete Hodgson’s classic article on martinfowler.com sorts flags into four categories by how long they live and how dynamic they are. Knowing which kind you are creating decides how you should manage it: Release toggles hide unfinished or risky code while it rolls out. They should live days or weeks, then be deleted. Experiment toggles split users into cohorts for A/B tests and must stay stable long enough to give meaningful results. Ops toggles let operators degrade or disable a feature during an incident. Most are short-lived, but a few kill switches stay forever. Permission toggles expose features to certain users, such as internal staff or paying customers, and can last for years. On the tooling side, OpenFeature is a CNCF project that standardises the API your code calls, while a provider plugs in the actual flag system. It became a CNCF incubating project in December 2023. The key terms: Provider: the adapter to a flag backend. We will use flagd, the open source flag engine from the OpenFeature project, but the same code works with commercial vendors that ship providers. Client: the object your code uses to evaluate flags, optionally scoped to a domain such as “checkout”. Evaluation context: the attributes a rule can use, such as user ID, plan or region. The targetingKey is the stable identifier used for percentage rollouts. Hooks: code that runs before, after or on error of every evaluation, ideal for logging and metrics. articles.title: I told Claude to hold off on isolation. Its networks took two of our LAN’s subnets.
articles.content: At 14:49 on October 13, I pasted two lines from a production host’s routing table into my Claude Code session: 192.168.16.0 0.0.0.0 255.255.240.0 U 0 0 0 br-f1a328c0938f 192.168.32.0 0.0.0.0 255.255.240.0 U 0 0 0 br-0adbee56597f Two /20 blocks, each sent to a Docker bridge. Machines on our LAN live in those ranges. From that host, traffic for anything between 192.168.16.0 and 192.168.47.255 went into the bridges instead of the network. I added one sentence, in French: “tu m’as fait un incident en prod”. You gave me a production incident. The first line of the answer said it was very probably its doing. It was. The part worth telling is what I had said before: I had asked to hold off on isolating that service, and the networks that broke the routes were the isolation. Some context. I run backend engineering at GoodBarber , an app platform. That morning, with Claude Code, I was putting a new internal service on two of our Docker hosts. Its spec said that one of its containers must eventually reach nothing on our network. I had given Claude the right to deploy through our Buildbot pipeline, and it wrote the deploy files and an isolation test that runs at every deploy. Where the subnets came from The compose file declared networks without a fixed range. When a network has no ipam subnet, Docker takes the next free block in its default pools: 172.17.0.0/16 to 172.31.0.0/16 first, then 192.168.0.0/16 cut into /20 blocks. On that host, the 172 ranges were already used, so the new networks landed in 192.168.0.0/16. Docker skips the blocks it knows are taken. Our hosts reach those two ranges through a router, so nothing on the host said they were in use. Each new bridge came with its own route, and from then on the host sent traffic for those ranges to the bridge. The networks appeared at 11:35, on the first deploy that got past the secrets step. They stayed until I stopped the service, a little after 14:50. For about three hours, that host’s traffic to two of our LAN’s ranges went nowhere. In practice, our failover took over, and end users saw nothing. What I had said, and when I went back through the session to see what Claude had been told. The times are Paris time, and the quotes are my translations. 11:23. The first deploy had failed, and I asked whether we could skip the iptables rule for now and add it just before the official release. Claude postponed the iptables rule. It kept the isolated networks from the spec, and the isolation test, which still failed the deploy if the container could reach the LAN, the Internet or DNS. Only the checks on the host itself became warnings. 11:46. About another part of the setup, I wrote that the LAN is private, that it shouldn’t overthink it, and that it should make something that works on the LAN. 12:09. Claude added a Redis container for the service, on a network of its own. I asked why it wanted one, then accepted it and asked to keep it isolated. That third network is on me. 13:37. I asked to put everything in production. Claude asked one question first, and the option it recommended put the iptables rule back and made the host check blocking. I said not to apply anything in production. 14:49. The two routes. 14:51. “I’m repeating my recommendation: don’t isolate it during the test phase.” Then I asked for a solution that obeyed me and left the routes alone, and said we would leave the isolation to ops. Read in order, my 11:23 message only named the iptables rule. Claude postponed exactly that and kept everything else the spec asked for. The spec was detailed and had been there since the start of the session. My instruction came later, in one sentence, about one mechanism. When the two disagreed, the spec won, and it went on winning at 13:37, when the recommended option brought back the rule I had postponed. Claude listened to my words and missed what I meant. It read “skip the iptables for now” as a list of one item, and kept the spec as the goal. What I meant was “no isolation during…

articles.title: My GPU fix was 13% faster on one card and 81% slower on another
articles.content: A vLLM int8 GEMM change, a reviewer with a smaller Ada GPU, and the one idea that explained it: waves On October 17 I opened a small vLLM pull request that made int8 matrix multiplies about 13% faster on an RTX 4090. The next day a reviewer ran it on a smaller Ada card and one layer got up to 81% slower. Same code, same kind of GPU, opposite result. This post is about why, and about the rule that fixed it on three different Ada GPUs. The PR is vLLM #62128 . It’s open and waiting for a maintainer’s review, so everything here is work in progress, not something that’s in vLLM yet. The bug report vLLM issue #56924 reported that int8 W8A8 GEMMs on Ada (SM89) get about 1.5x slower when the number of tokens M goes from 16 to 17, and again from 32 to 33. That’s the batch range a server lives in during decode, so it matters. The cause was in the dispatch code that picks a CUTLASS tile shape based on M: For the small layers of a model like Qwen3–1.7B (N = 2048), bigger tiles mean fewer thread blocks. With 64-column tiles, N = 2048 gives 32 tiles across. At M = 17 with 32-row tiles that’s 32 thread blocks in total, on a GPU with 128 SMs. Most of the GPU sits idle, and each block does twice the work. On my RTX 4090, q_proj jumped from 4.92 µs at M = 16 to 7.81 µs at M = 17. The first fix The obvious fix: keep the 16-row tiles past M = 16 for small layers. More, smaller blocks, more of the GPU busy. I used an N limit to decide what “small” meant (N ≤ 4096 for M up to 32, N ≤ 2048 up to 64), measured it on the 4090, and the numbers were good: about 13% less total GEMM time over M = 17–64 across six Qwen3–1.7B shapes (409.5 → 355.3 µs) q_proj at M = 17: 7.81 → 5.53 µs identical results, all 400 int8 tests passing I opened the PR and wrote in the description that I had only measured it on a 4090. The review The next day Shikha Pallavi ran it on an RTX 4500 Ada and posted every number on the PR. qkv_proj got 21% faster. But down_proj got 35–81% slower at every M the change touched, and o_proj at M = 64 got 24% slower. The RTX 4500 Ada has 60 SMs. The 4090 has 128. That turned out to be the whole story. Waves A GPU runs thread blocks on its SMs. If there are more blocks than can run at once, the extra ones wait and run in a second round, a second wave . The kernel isn’t done until the last wave finishes. For these int8 kernels the tiles use a lot of shared memory (51–80 KB against Ada’s 100 KB per SM), so each SM runs one block at a time. That makes the math simple: waves = ceil(blocks / SMs). Take down_proj (N = 2048) at M = 17: On the 4090, 64 smaller blocks all run at once and finish sooner. That’s the 13%. On the 4500 Ada, 60 of them run, then the last 4 run alone while 56 SMs wait. Each block is faster, but you pay for a whole extra round. That’s the slowdown. Looking back at my own 4090 data, every case where the 16-row tiles had lost was a case where they added a wave. I’d picked an N limit that happened to avoid those on 128 SMs. On 60 SMs it didn’t. I put the PR back in draft and thanked the reviewer. They were right, and they’d tested it on hardware I didn’t have. The new rule Instead of guessing from N, count the waves. The dispatch now reads the SM count once per device and uses the 16-row tiles only when: they fit in the same number of waves as the stock tiles, or the stock tiles already need two or more waves, and the 16-row tiles add at most half again as many. waves_16 = ceil(ceil(M / 16) * n_tiles / SMs) waves_stock = ceil(ceil(M / stock_rows) * n_tiles / SMs) use 16-row tiles if waves_16 == waves_stock or (waves_stock >= 2 and 2 * waves_16 <= 3 * waves_stock) The second part exists for one case: qkv_proj (N = 4096) on a 60-SM card goes from 2 waves to 3, and it was still faster in the reviewer's run. When the GPU is already doing several rounds, smaller blocks fill the last round better. That 1.5x allowance is the one part of the rule fitted to data, so it needed checking on real hardware. On the 4090 the new rule picks…

articles.title: The next great founder may be hiding in healthcare
articles.content: Academic medical centers and universities produce groundbreaking research every day. An autism researcher who builds an AI game to clinically improve behavioral problems. A basic scientist who discovers how the environment of tumors impacts treatment. An electrical engineer who nano-sized a method for magnets to image the body. An MBA who teamed up with two MDs to create a novel approach to solving complex pediatric cardiac cases. And all are at risk of remaining stuck in the ivory tower. Venture capital is great at finding founders who tell a compelling story with confidence, but the best founders may not innately exhibit those traits. This is particularly true in healthcare, where physicians, researchers, PhDs, and faculty members often have the deep technical understanding and firsthand experience needed to build the next great company. These scientists and clinicians are knee-deep in the problems they’re trying to solve. They’ve seen where existing approaches fall short, often for years, and have developed ideas for how to do things differently. But getting those ideas into the market requires a different set of skills. They need to learn how to test the market hypothesis, not just the scientific hypothesis. Today, there are researchers and scientists developing promising healthcare innovations who aren’t thinking about building a company. And if they are, many show up to pitch venture capitalists with presentations better suited for an academic keynote or scientific meeting. Slides dense in technical detail, with little market analysis or validation, and without much of a story. It’s not surprising that many VCs pass. But how many promising ideas are we missing because the people behind them haven’t learned how to pitch? Our experience We’ve seen this firsthand, over and over again. And it’s made us rethink what it actually means to invest early. Funds have competed for years to get into the best deals as early as possible. But in healthcare, getting in early may mean investing before there’s even a company. Before there’s a pitch deck, a business model, or a founder who has fully embraced the idea of becoming an entrepreneur. This is the idea behind inception investing. Rather than starting with a company and evaluating whether it’s worth backing, the starting point is a person who is particularly well suited to solving a problem. That might be a clinician or researcher with decades of experience and a scientific approach that hasn’t yet been commercialized. Or it might be someone whose personal experience with the healthcare system has led them to become deeply focused on a problem that others have overlooked. In either case, there may be no company yet. The market might not be defined. The founder might not know how to tell a compelling story. But those aren’t necessarily reasons to walk away. At Treehub, we’ve found that the qualities we’re looking for in these early conversations are often different from what a traditional investor might prioritize. We’re less concerned with whether someone can deliver a polished pitch and more interested in whether they understand a problem well enough to build something that hasn’t existed before. More than just science Of course, scientific expertise alone doesn’t make a successful founder. There still needs to be a market for the solution, a viable business model, and a path to getting it into patients’ hands. And not every researcher wants to build a company. But those are questions worth exploring with someone who has spent years developing a potentially important solution, rather than reasons to dismiss them at the outset. A scientist can learn how to evaluate a market. A physician can find a commercial partner. A researcher can learn how to tell a story that resonates with investors. The experience that led them to the idea in the first place is much harder to…

articles.title: PsiQuantum turns its photonics know-how into an optical switch for supercharging AI data center GPU networks
articles.content: PsiQuantum, a quantum computing company, announced in a release earlier this week that it has turned its low-loss silicon photonics into an optical switch for use in AI data centers. Every optical switch typically comes with loss of light: the more light a switch receives, the less reaches the other side, with the amount of light lost measured in decibels. Typical data center optics can tolerate half the light (3 dB) being lost. PsiQuantum's switch debuted with a demo that typically loses only 1.2 dB of signal, or about a quarter of the light in lab tests, and the all-optical switch can achieve it without an amplifier. The prototype is, however, comparatively small, with eight inputs and outputs (8x8) against competitors’ 32 to 300, but the company says larger devices are in development. The optical circuit switch (OCS) passes light straight through, from fiber to fiber, without converting it to or from electrical signals. Regular data center switches make that conversion at every hop, which takes power and adds latency. An OCS, instead, uses a fixed light path that it maintains until a change is ordered. Its main penalty comes down to how much light is lost when passing through the switch. PsiQuantum’s switch, which uses circuits etched on a silicon chip with no moving parts, unlike Google’s and Lumentum’s tiny mirrors, or microelectromechanical systems (MEMS), would be used alongside regular packet switches. Skipping those conversions matters more as AI clusters grow, because moving data between GPUs is quickly becoming a bottleneck. Optics are a high-bandwidth improvement over copper, which has limitations in reach, although a shortage of lasers is a problem for the alternative. Improving communication bandwidth and distance is the goal, so that different racks of GPUs can talk at speed and act as one. Switches similar to PsiQuantum’s made by Salience Labs and iPronics use built-in amplification and, at least in the former case, are also rated at under 2 dB, or under 37% of the light lost. Google’s mirror-based switch , Palomar, can also typically stay under 2 dB and has 136 ports. Salience’s switch sits at 32 and Lumentum’s at 300, which leaves the eight-port prototype a ways behind on how many fibers it can handle. In the lab, it measured a typical 1.2 dB insertion loss, 40 dB of crosstalk (about 0.01% of the light leaking to other ports), and under 3 ms of reconfiguration time, all of which exceed “initial targets set for these devices.” The loss figure is measured fiber to fiber, which includes getting light onto and off the chip but not connector losses, PsiQuantum told Tom’s Hardware Premium . The platform loses very little light at each component, which matters because a quantum computer can tolerate only so much lost light. articles.title: Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available
articles.content: Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection . Your origin stays private, while web application firewall ( WAF ), caching , bot management , and Workers work just as they do for public origins. In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin. Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers. What is generally available today During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group. Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins: WAF and managed rules Bot management Rate limiting Caching Transform and rewrite rules Workers Some limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Dedicated CDN Egress IPs aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing . See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations. Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN , no connector software on the origin is required. With Cloudflare Mesh , a connector runs within your private network and can serve multiple origins. How it works Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually. The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network. The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error. What the API looks like For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record. POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records { "type": "A", "name": "app.example.com", "content": "10.0.0.50", "ttl": 300, "proxied": true, "private_routing": true } Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path: { "zone_name": "example.com", "ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"], "private_routing": true } The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec , GRE , Cloudflare Tunnel , CNI , or Cloudflare Mesh. The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail. Get started Before you begin, you’ll need: The Private Origins entitlement on your account. Ask your account team to turn it on. Cloudflare One connectivity using IPsec, GRE, CNI, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Cloudflare Mesh . Unified Routing enabled on your account, unless you connect over Cloudflare Tunnel (Tunnel…

articles.title: TCL 27C2A Pro 27-inch QD-Mini LED 4K gaming monitor review: Extreme color and brightness
articles.content: You’ve probably heard TCL’s name associated with jumbo TVs sold in big-box stores, but it also makes a line of gaming monitors that offer excellent performance for the money. It’s also one of the few companies putting effort into Mini LED panels where others have gone all-in with OLED. Mini LED delivers the brightest imagery you can buy among the best gaming monitors , with HDR peaks of 2,000 nits or more. TCL’s 27C2A Pro is such a panel, with an honest 2,000 nits from a 3% window in HDR mode and 650 nits full field for SDR. It also sports a full-array local dimming (FALD) backlight with 2,304 zones, which delivers tremendous contrast. A Quantum Dot layer pushes the color gamut past 100% of DCI-P3. And a set of accurate picture modes promise precise color rendering. It’s speedy too, with 160 Hz in 4K and 320 Hz in FHD resolution , with available overdrive and MPRT backlight strobing. This fully loaded package can be yours for $600 as I write this. Let’s take a look. TCL 27C2A Pro Specs Panel Type / Backlight Quantum Dot IPS / Mini LED 2,304 dimming zones Screen Size / Aspect Ratio 27 inches / 16:9 Max Resolution and Refresh Rate 3840x2160 @ 160 Hz 1920x1080 @ 320 Hz FreeSync and G-Sync Compatible Native Color Depth and Gamut 10-bit (8-bit+FRC) / DCI-P3+ Response Time (GTG) 0.2ms Brightness (mfr) 600 nits full field 2,000 nits 3% window Contrast (mfr) 1,000:1 Speakers 2x 5w Video Inputs 1x DisplayPort 1.4 2x HDMI 2.1, 1x Type C Audio 3.5mm headphone output USB 3.0 1x up, 2x down Power Consumption 36.1w, brightness @ 200 nits Panel Dimensions WxHxD w/base 24.2 x 15.7-20.5 x 9 inches (615 x 399-521 x 229mm) Panel Thickness 3.27 inches (83mm) Bezel Width Top/sides: 0.35 inch (9mm) Bottom: 0.59 inches (15mm) Weight 14.6 pounds (6.64kg) Warranty 3 years The 27C2A Pro’s core tech is an IPS variant TCL calls HFS Shoot. It combines an ultra-bright FALD backlight with Quantum Dot color and very quick response. Native resolution is 4K 3840x2160 pixels for a density of 163ppi. This is about as fine as it gets unless you move up to 5K or more. And those panels are still quite rare and expensive. Brightness is honestly reported here, with my tests matching TCL’s claims. I saw almost 650 nits from a full white field pattern in SDR mode with the dimming turned off. HDR ran that up to almost 1,700 nits when I measured a 25% window with dimming on High. At that setting, I couldn’t measure the black levels at all. With 2,304 dimming zones, you won’t see any halo artifacts like panels with just a few hundred zones. The Quantum Dot layer delivers just over 100% of the DCI-P3 gamut. You also get accurate picture modes with presets for DCI-P3 , sRGB , Rec.709, and Adobe RGB, which is something rarely found outside the professional realm. Accuracy is superb with little to no need for calibration. I found similarly good performance in HDR mode, where you can adjust grayscale tracking and brightness if you wish. The 27C2A Pro offers premium gaming too, with 160 Hz in 4K and 320 Hz in FHD resolution with a dual-mode switch. And there’s precise overdrive, Adaptive-Sync, and MPRT backlight strobing. This is one of the few monitors that lets you use all its video processing options at the same time. You can have MPRT, Adaptive-Sync, and overdrive all active at once. Styling is outside the norm as well, with a white aesthetic for the stand and panel’s backside. LED lighting shines in the back with two large bracket shapes that show an array of colors and effects. There are gaming aids like reticles, timers, and a frame rate indicator. And you get a full complement of I/O ports with HDMI 2.1 , DisplayPort 1.4 , and a USB-C, plus USB for your peripherals. Assembly and Accessories The 27C2A Pro ships in blocks of crumbly foam in its three main parts: base, upright, and panel. They assemble without tools. Under the snap-on fulcrum is a 100mm VESA mount with fasteners included if you'd rather use an arm, and you might want to after you read the next section of…

articles.title: NASA ponders a Hubble servicing mission or a controlled deorbit
articles.content: NASA has posted a contract opportunity notice, also known as a request for information, from commercial space orgs who can service the Hubble Space Telescope. Hubble was always looked after by NASA astronauts flying on the Space Shuttle, yet the last Hubble Space Telescope (HST) servicing mission was the STS-125 Space Shuttle flight, launched on May 11, 2009. At the time, scientists hoped the mission would add another five years of operational life to the venerable spacecraft. Almost 17 years on, the HST (aka Hubble) is still delivering science. However, time is running out for the observatory. NASA reckons there is a 10 percent chance it could reenter the Earth's atmosphere by September 2032, rising to 50 percent by December 2033. As the end of the Swift mission showed, increased solar activity can cause greater-than-anticipated atmospheric drag. Also, like Swift, Hubble has no propulsion system, and so when it reenters (as it will, without intervention), the reentry will be uncontrolled. Hubble is sufficiently massive that there is a remote chance somebody on the ground could have a very bad day when that happens. As such, one mission option suggested by NASA is a vehicle to grapple the observatory and perform a controlled reentry and disposal. However, there are other options. Something to boost the telescope's orbit up to at least 600 km, or another to "enhance its ongoing performance and increase its resilience and expected on-orbit lifetime." Both are intriguing options, and important since, as NASA acknowledges, no replacement for Hubble is expected before the 2040s, when the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) could become operational. Despite the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Nancy Roman Space Telescope, Hubble remains in high demand, with NASA reporting a 7:1 oversubscription. Before becoming NASA Administrator, Jared Isaacman advocated a SpaceX mission to boost the Hubble, but the idea was ultimately rejected. Similar plans could now be dusted off. NASA's requirement is for a mission to occur by 2032, and not harm the Hubble. A soft-capture mechanism was fitted to Hubble during the STS-125 mission, which will mean docking with the spacecraft will be easier than the grappling planned for Swift. Then, the question is what to do with it. A controlled reentry is one option. The other options – boosting to a higher altitude or "enhance its ongoing performance and increase its resilience" are intriguing. Northrop Grumman's Mission Extension Vehicle (MEV) , for example, is capable of on-orbit servicing and extending the lifetime of satellites. The Hubble is an order of magnitude more challenging, but the technological hurdles can be overcome with time and funding. Last year, The Register spoke with Dr John Grunsfeld, one of the astronauts (now retired) who worked on Hubble during the STS-125 mission. Grunsfeld told us that the veteran spacecraft faced death by a thousand cuts as its budget was whittled away. The observatory itself recently switched from three to one gyro mode (the telescope uses gyros to control where it is pointed) to eke out a few more years of operational life. At this point, NASA is looking for information and comment – this isn't a request for proposals. There is no indication of how much the agency expects to pay. However, the timescale is immutable. Without intervention, Hubble will make an uncontrolled reentry in the coming years. ®

articles.title: GM to pay $220 million after selling customer Smart Driver data
articles.content: General Motors marketed its Smart Driver system as a way for parents to monitor teen drivers or for adults to track their driving behavior. But in 2024, it emerged that GM had been sharing that data with brokers. Those brokers then sold the data to insurance companies , and some drivers found that their insurance became more expensive as a result. To make matters worse, many of those drivers claimed they had no knowledge of ever agreeing to share such data for such purposes. Last year , GM and its OnStar subsidiary entered into a settlement with the FTC, prohibiting them from sharing some kinds of driver data with third parties. The settlement was finalized this January. That agreement banned the two companies from sharing geolocation data or driver behavior data for five years. At the time, GM also discontinued Smart Driver across its entire range. Now the automaker has reached terms with the District of Columbia and 35 states after their attorneys general joined together to sue GM as well. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Intelligence agency misplaced 'a very significant number' of removable drives
articles.content: The UK’s Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office (IPCO) has flagged “a very significant number” of General Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) storage drives that have been missing for years and have yet to be found. According to The Register , the lost storage media have been known to GCHQ officials for years now, but they’re still unsure about the scope of the problem. "I remain concerned that GCHQ has not yet established a sufficiently clear understanding of the scale, location, and recoverability of lost removable media that may contain IPA-related data, notwithstanding that the underlying issues were first drawn to my attention several years ago. While I recognize the technical and practical challenges involved, the passage of time without a comprehensive account heightens the importance of sustained senior focus and assured remediation. Given the potential sensitivity of the material involved, I will continue to monitor progress closely,” investigatory powers commissioner Lord Brian Leveson wrote in the report. GCHQ acknowledged to The Register that the tracking system for its removable media had been insufficient, but it has since taken steps to prevent it happening in the future. "We recognize the importance of security of removable media in our systems and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items. The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively, and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken," a GCHQ spokesperson told the publication. It has also launched a program to help locate as many of the lost storage media as possible and will have an automated asset-tracking system up and running before 2027. The GCHQ is the UK’s equivalent to the National Security Agency (NSA), making it the country’s primary signals intelligence and cybersecurity agency. Its primary mission is governed by the Investigatory Powers Act (IPA), which was passed in 2016 and lays out the legal framework for government surveillance, data collection, and intercepting communications. While neither agency has exactly confirmed what data the missing drives contained, it could potentially have information about GCHQ operations, administration, and other crucial data. While the UK’s premier signals intelligence and cybersecurity agency losing thousands of removable drives may sound alarming, it’s not alone in running into blunders like this. The publication reported that Britain’s Ministry of Defence has lost 87 classified USB drives from 2003 to 2008, and that the UK police have also dealt with officers losing their assigned tech gadgets. Other governments have also made considerable tech missteps — for example, the South Korean government lost 858TB of data after a catastrophic fire destroyed a data center, and it discovered that it had no backups. Indonesia discovered the same issue when it was hit with a ransomware attack , with one government official calling the lack of backups “stupid.”

articles.title: A primer on key AI LLM concepts — KV cache, weights, quantization, and how inference actually works
articles.content: As hardware for running local AI models continues to move to the forefront, such as Nvidia's RTX Spark, a new set of acronyms, definitions, and terminology is popping up. Given the pace of releases, we've put together a list of AI's new nomenclature to familiarize you with new concepts and pieces of terminology that you'll likely see in Tom's Hardware Premium articles. This primer should get you started on the world of AI and be handy the next time news on the topic comes around, and possibly when you're downloading some models to try out and tweak for yourself. For the context of this article, we're going to stick with notions related to text LLMs, or in common parlance, chat, programming, and most agentic bots. Model This is probably the easiest one: a model is the LLM itself (a Large Language Model), computed from training sets of mostly text data on the scale of terabytes to petabytes. That training information comes from the internet, books, video and audio transcripts, and other sources. The model is roughly analogous to a set of highly advanced layers of statistical analysis of relationships between tokens — words or parts of words, computer code, punctuation, and other symbols. The tokens themselves aren't part of the model, but they are packaged along with it. An AI model generates tokens in its outputs. Weights Those computing layers within an AI model would be useless without corresponding weights , which represent how strong the connection is between sections of tokens, sort of like how a pathway between neurons is more traveled than others. When the model runs, these values end up establishing how tokens end up relating to each other. Example: the weights of the connections between "na" and each next part for "naval", "nachos", or "naruto" will all be different, and the higher the weight, the more often that word appears in training data. Importantly, weights cannot change without re-training the model, or parts of it. When you see LLM specs online, you'll see something like "4B", "8B+", "20B", and so on and so forth. That shows how many parameters, or weights, the model uses, and it's generally measured in billions for consumer-grade models, and trillions for frontier models like GPT, Claude, and Kimi. Note that a model having more weights than another doesn't automatically mean it's smarter. Just like with CPU clock speeds, it's not just about getting a higher number — bigger is usually better, yes, but you want those weights to be meaningful for the output. You may also have heard about " open-weight " models versus " closed " models. Those refer to models like Llama, DeepSeek, and Kimi, which are effectively free-to-use, since the entities behind them freely publish the weights online. You can tweak the weights to your heart's content, if you wish, and come up with your own spin on things, as long as you have the hardware to run it. Note that downloading a free model doesn't reveal anything about how it was trained or how the weights were calculated — think downloading a free customizable application, not open-source software. Data types and quantization FP16, INT8, FP4, all sound like acronyms in some military handbook, but they're simple to interpret. All programs use numbers of varying width and precision, depending on their purpose: a simple money counter in your favorite game might be fine with a 32-bit integer that can represent 0 to 2^32 (INT32), while a value held in memory for a highly precise scientific measurement may need floating-point 64-bit arithmetic (FP64). As memory is an exceedingly finite resource, good developers try to use the smallest units they can get away with, a notion that's particularly important in the VRAM-limited world of GPUs. Predictably, these chips became particularly adept at handling lower-precision values as a tradeoff between processing speed and numerical accuracy. A particular datatype isn't better or worse, as that assessment will depend on what it's used for. When…

articles.title: AI projects not paying off? Keep at it, says Uni Productivity Institute
articles.content: The University of Manchester is scrutinizing why growing adoption of AI tools has so far failed to translate into the forecast productivity gains, however, researchers are struggling to give easy answers to close the "AI ambition gap." In a report, also called “ The AI Ambition Gap ,” the UK university’s Productivity Institute mulls over the advances that have been made in AI and the expanding adoption of it, and sets out what business leaders and policymakers can do to realize the potential benefits. The report was commissioned by IT services biz Bytes Technology Group . One reason for the lack of results is that organizations have invested heavily up front on retraining staff, reorganizing the way they work and other adjustments. Those costs show up straight away, yet the payback doesn’t come until later. Another reason, the report suggests, is that AI tools can raise productivity at the level of individual tasks, but these gains do not automatically translate into greater productivity across a worker’s whole role or the entire organization. It cites the example of software developers using GitHub Copilot who completed around 26 percent more tasks, and professionals using ChatGPT for routine writing and analysis that reduced task completion time by 40 percent while improving the quality of the output by 18 percent. However, a study of AI dev tools found these have increased coding activity by approximately 240 percent, while the number of actual software releases has only grown by about 30 percent. The gap is due to humans still needing to check and test their work before release. High task exposure to AI does not automatically make a worker more productive, the researchers say. Jobs typically combine automatable activities with tasks that require judgement, coordination, client interaction and critical thinking. As AI removes or accelerates some activities, those complementary human tasks become the constraint on time saving and the translation of task-level gains into greater productivity Job outcomes therefore depend on task composition and complementary human expertise, the report continues. It suggests AI may in part displace labor from existing tasks, while also creating new tasks in which workers retain a comparative advantage. This could be good news for the UK, the researchers state. Compared with five other nations (US, Brazil, Colombia, India and South Africa), Blighty has the highest share of workers in occupations with both high exposure to AI and "high complementarity," it claims. This is in part related to the country’s large financial and professional business service sectors, which are characterized by a high share of cognitive occupations. This is just as well, as the government is pinning its hopes on using AI to drive economic recovery in a strategy outlined at the start of last year. Britain's AI sector is relatively large by European standards, and the report cites recent OECD estimates that high-exposure economies such as the UK and the US could see annual labor productivity gains of between 0.4 and 1.3 percentage points. Even an annual uplift of around 0.5 to 0.7 percentage points would represent a significant step change relative to the UK’s stalled productivity performance over the past decade, it says, if this effect is sustained. The Productivity Institute lists several "mutually reinforcing enablers" to help organizations close the ambition gap it identifies. None is particularly surprising, especially if you have read other reports advising on corporate success with AI adoption. One is management setting strategic direction for the organization, another is strengthening worker capabilities through greater knowledge and data literacy to help organizations turn individual insight into shared learning. Others include implementing AI governance and focusing on applications that can create new products, improve core processes or solve previously intractable problems. "AI's productivity potential…

articles.title: How a Bank Serving 100 Million Users Tests Agentic AI in Production
articles.content: TL;DR : A KDD 2026 paper follows five customer support AI agents through testing and deployment. The team checks automated graders against expert judgments, starts new versions at 1% to 5% exposure, and tracks whether satisfaction gains come with more self-service or more work for human agents. An automated grader can give an AI agent a passing score and still be wrong. In a June 2026 paper accepted to ACM’s KDD 2026 conference , engineers at a digital bank report that one grader initially performed worse than simply choosing the most common answer. Before relying on it to evaluate customer-facing agents, they had to improve the evaluator itself. The paper describes how a bank serving more than 100 million users tests agentic AI in production across card delivery, debt management, credit limits, card management and product explanation. That customer base provides context for the deployment; it is not the test sample size. For companies buying agentic AI, the case offers a view into how a team decides an agent is ready to handle more work. The evidence comes from customer support, rather than paid media or back-office workflows. Its useful contribution is the detail behind each readiness decision, from the tests a new version must pass to the point where a person takes over. All Five AI Agents Improved Satisfaction but Scored Below Human Benchmarks All five agents improved transactional Net Promoter Score (tNPS), collected after a support interaction, in online A/B tests. The comparison varied by agent, including earlier versions and a control group. Scores nevertheless remained below the bank’s expert human-agent benchmarks, which were measured separately within the support funnel. Agent Satisfaction Self-service Compared with human agents Card delivery Large gain Largest gain Behind Debt management Largest gain Small gain Furthest behind Credit limit Small gain Moderate gain Close behind Card management Large gain Small gain Nearly matched Product explainer Moderate gain Slight dip Close behind Source: Gupta et al., KDD 2026, Table 3. Human scores were measured separately from the AI scores. The self-service rate tracks how many requests the AI resolved without handing them to a person. Card delivery posted the largest gain, 29 percentage points, alongside a 37-point rise in satisfaction. The product explainer was the one exception, with a slight dip the authors attribute to temporary errors in calls to the language model. The Automated Grader Initially Scored Below a Simple Baseline The team separates an agent’s instructions and business procedures into modules that can be revised individually. Domain experts change those modules, then language models acting as automated graders evaluate candidate versions before live testing. To establish the reference answers, three operations analysts labeled each evaluation sample and explained their decisions. Majority vote determined the final label. Those explanations then helped GEPA, a prompt-optimization method, refine the graders’ instructions. On customer input verification, the initial grader scored 68.88% accuracy. Always choosing the most common label would have scored 77.78%. Optimization raised accuracy to 88.89%, measuring agreement with the expert labels rather than the customer-facing agent’s overall accuracy. The authors also tested whether different grader models agreed after optimization. Those tests covered models from one vendor, leaving broader model coverage for future work. New Agent Versions Start With 1% to 5% Exposure Offline checks let the team test targeted fixes before exposing customers to them. Live metrics then reveal problems those checks missed, including changes in escalation patterns. New versions begin at 1% to 5% exposure while the team tracks self-service, tNPS, escalations and errors. The bank’s agents transfer conversations to people when a request falls outside their routines, necessary data cannot be retrieved or confidence is low. According…

articles.title: What five P99 CONF talks reveal about database trade-offs
articles.content: P99 CONF is a virtual conference on high-performance, low-latency applications. Its 2026 event ran October 21–22 . Here, we cover five of its 60-plus sessions. The recordings are available on demand at p99conf.io after registration. Database storage design balances read amplification , write amplification, and space amplification (RUM conjecture). Improving one can increase another, depending on the workload and configuration. The five talks below show how engineers make those trade-offs across different database systems. “Can Everything be an LSM?” Almog Gavra , Co-Founder at Responsive (now Databricks) Gavra frames database design around read amplification (data read per result), write amplification (data written per logical write), and space amplification (storage used relative to live data). A log favors fast writes but makes reads work harder; a sorted array does the reverse. As Gavra put it, “I think about LSM trees as a mechanism for tuning between these two extremes.” LSMs were built for local disks, but their immutable files also fit object storage. Gavra points to Amazon S3’s lower storage cost, durability, and availability, then names the trade-offs: objects must be replaced rather than edited, each GET and PUT has a price, and cold reads are slower. In his example, a local NVMe cache miss takes about 150 microseconds, versus 20–30 milliseconds for S3 Standard — roughly two orders of magnitude. LSMs batch writes into immutable files; caching helps keep object-store reads off the hot path. Gavra’s SlateDB is an open-source, object-store-native LSM library. It exposes a key-value interface over stores such as S3, GCS, and R2, so developers can build data systems without implementing their own LSM. How ScyllaDB Eliminates Read Amplification at Scale Michael Litvak (Senior Software Engineer) and Felipe Cardeneti Mendes (Technical Director), ScyllaDB ScyllaDB’s presentation examines Logstor , an opt-in storage engine for read-intensive key-value workloads, not a replacement for its existing LSM engine. For each key, an in-memory index stores a hash and the record’s location on flash. A read can return a cached value or find the record with one disk I/O, avoiding an LSM search across SSTables, Bloom Filters, and Indexed data structures. Tables using either engine can run in the same cluster with ScyllaDB’s existing drivers and consistency options. The speakers’ preliminary read-dominant test sustained 1.1 million reads per second with p99.9 latency below one millisecond and p99.99 latency around 1.5 milliseconds. That test used 2 KB values; the earlier LSM examples in the talk used 1 KB values, so the results are not direct comparisons. They also reported similar throughput and sub-millisecond p99.9 latency in an 80% read, 20% write workload. Logstor pays for those reads with a larger RAM index and more work on writes. Even a small update writes the full new value to a log, leaving the old record as dead space; segment compaction later reclaims it. The speaker positions it for bounded key sets, frequent overwrites, and point lookups where the extra memory is acceptable. During this talk, Mendes called the trade-off “optimized for time at the sacrifice of space.” The Vertical Scaling Wall, and How Valkey Gets Over It Madelyn Olson , Principal Software Engineer at AWS Not every bottleneck is storage. Olson begins with Amazon ElastiCache customers who saw sudden p50 latency spikes, then tests where Valkey’s main execution thread reached its limit. In Olson’s unpipelined GET benchmark, with about three million keys and 650 clients, p50 latency rose sharply near 150,000 requests per second. Valkey already had I/O threads , but they sat idle while the main thread executed commands. The team used lockless queues to keep network I/O and command parsing active on those threads while command execution stayed on the main thread.…

articles.title: NHS quango warns of risk to GP patient data after website vendor collapse
articles.content: The UK's top health quango has called on family doctors to figure out how to preserve health information and get in touch with patients after a website provider collapsed earlier this month. NHS England has taken the unusual step of writing to GPs, warning them of the risks to patient information and continuity of service following the disruption to potentially hundreds of practices around the UK. Silicon Practice Digital Health Solutions — owned by Schappit Ltd — has gone into administration . Reports suggest some GP websites have gone offline completely. Practice managers fear the extra workload and are struggling to stand up alternative forms of communication since the switch to digital channels. NHS England is the government unit which runs the health service in England, but it is not directly responsible for GP practices, the vast majority of which are independent contractors. Nonetheless, the quango’s CTO, Kevin Humphries, wrote to practices and NHS organizations this week outlining his priorities in mitigating the impact of tech service collapse. They include finding ways of preserving any historical patient information, particularly where it has not been moved to clinical systems, managing the online consultation backlog to make sure no additional requests are added, and identifying channels for patient access until new online systems are available. Practices should also consider whether they have a legal obligation to tell the Information Commissioner's Office if the "availability, integrity, confidentiality or recoverability of personal data" is affected, according to the communication seen by The Register . NHS management bodies called Integrated Care Boards are responsible for GP IT service arrangements, making sure they include "clinical safety, data security, cyber security and business continuity assurance across the GP IT supply chain," Humphries said. They need to find someone to lead their recovery plan and contact affected practices and trusts. They should also "work with practices and other impacted organizations to support them in revisiting and assessing whether to enact business continuity and disaster recovery plans," Humphries said. Questions over how an urgent NHS-wide response is required for the collapse of a relatively small supplier may come later. Among them will be the due diligence conducted before Schappit Ltd was added to a government framework in July . GP and open-source tech campaigner Marcus Baw has published a free, open source template for an alternative website should practices want to bring systems in-house. He said the template is based on accessible NHS web standards, and has the same look-and-feel of common NHS websites. "Practices can deploy it for free, and take back in-house control of their own website. It's a replacement website template which practices can set up using Claude Code in the web in an afternoon," he said. ®
