articles.title: 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid: Drives like an EV, but there's no plug involved
articles.content: Nissan provided flights from Washington, DC, to Santa Barbara, California, and accommodation so Ars could drive the Rogue Hybrid. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. Nissan has a new version of its bestselling Rogue SUV, and it’s launching the model here with the latest version of its e-Power hybrid system, which Ars tested in February. Most hybrid cars you can buy today are parallel hybrids, which means that they have an internal combustion engine and an electric motor, both of which drive some or all of the wheels—everything works in parallel. But there’s another approach. Instead of connecting the engine to the wheels via a transmission, it can act as a generator and charge the traction battery, which in turn powers the electric motor. Since the engine and motor work in series, this is known as a series hybrid. That’s mostly how the Chevrolet Volt worked. As does Honda’s hybrid CR-V . Well, mostly; engineers worked out it was more efficient for those cars' gasoline engines to directly drive the wheels at highway speeds, something that to this day makes a certain subset of hybrid car enthusiasts irrationally angry. If you know anyone like that in your life, send them to wherever the nearest Nissan dealership is, because the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is exactly what they’ve been asking for. Series hybrids Under the hood, with its crisp shut line and slim horizontal lights that give me something of a Range Rover vibe, there’s a 1.5 L, three-cylinder turbocharged direct-injection engine that generates 148 hp (110 kW). It only revs to 5,200 rpm because it’s optimized to charge the battery, not cope with the various loads of an engine connected to a gearbox and the wheels. That also allows the engine to operate at a rather impressive 42 percent thermal efficiency—we would need to look at Formula 1 engines to find higher. Read full article Comments

articles.title: I tried plug-in solar and loved it—but there’s a catch
articles.content: Getting solar installed on your roof typically involves weeks of planning and red tape and hiring an installation crew to do the work. I tried a very different option: a plug-in solar panel. Like the name implies, installing it essentially just means plugging it into an outdoor wall yourself. Then power starts flowing back into your house. A single panel, of course, generates a tiny fraction of what you’d get from a full rooftop system. But it’s still a simple way to begin to offset your electric bill , and it’s something that renters can use, not just homeowners. This year, states have started rolling out a wave of new laws designed to clear the way for plug-in solar. I wanted to see how easy it was to use. [Photo: Bright Saver] How plug-in solar works I tested a kit from Bright Saver , a nonprofit that advocates for plug-in solar. The 180-watt solar panel is somewhat large, at 4 by 3 feet, but lightweight and easy to move. You can attach it to a wall or fence, or buy a small separate stand so it can sit at an angle on the ground. In the back, the panel plugs into an inverter, a small box that converts the current from the solar panels into electricity that you can use in your house. The inverter plugs into the wall. Unlike portable solar panels designed for camping, which typically work with a battery, this system is designed to sync with the grid, pushing current into your outlet at the exact frequency and voltage of the grid signal. If grid power goes out, the inverter shuts down in milliseconds, so there’s no risk of the solar panel sending electricity back into the grid when utility workers are fixing an outage on a line. My first challenge was where to plug it in, since my 180-year-old house didn’t have outdoor outlets. When I started looking around for where wiring could be added—a process that involved opening a trap door and discovering a second, hidden basement—I realized that reaching the sunniest wall would be too difficult. The only easily accessible spot for my electrician to add an outlet was on an eastern wall; ideally, to generate the most energy, panels should face south or southwest. Still, it was a reasonably sunny place to test. The kit was fast to set up. It took only a few minutes to plug everything together, and to begin testing it, I propped it up temporarily rather than trying to attach it to the wall. After a couple of minutes, the inverter started flashing green. Power was beginning to flow. The app for the kit was clunky, and repeatedly failed to connect to the system. But it finally recognized the inverter, then showed on the screen exactly how much power the solar panel was sending back into my house. I live in upstate New York, and late October isn’t the sunniest time of year. When I first connected the system, early on a hazy morning with no direct light on the panel, it generated only 8 watts—roughly enough to power my WiFi router. Later in the morning, as it got sunnier, the output jumped up to 81 watts, more than enough to power my fridge or my MacBook Air. The solar panel might only reach its peak of 180 watts under the right conditions in the summer. But even on a fall day, it was able to provide a meaningful chunk of the power I was using. Bright Saver offers the kit with either one 180-watt solar panel ($285 for members; $499 for nonmembers) or two, for a total of 360 watts. The panels are designed to last for 20 years, and depending on your electricity rates, can pay for themselves in savings within the first couple of years. With a single small panel, you’re unlikely to produce extra power beyond what your house uses. If you use multiple panels and don’t have a battery, any extra power that you don’t use goes back into the grid. While your utility won’t pay you for it, it could eventually help you in an indirect way: If solar panels like these were used by large numbers of people, it could help shrink the load on the grid at times of peak demand. articles.title: British intelligence agency misplaced 'thousands' of storage devices, years later still can't say how many
articles.content: Thousands of GCHQ storage drives containing sensitive data have been lost for years, and the British signals intelligence agency still cannot explain where they are. According to the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office’s (IPCO) annual report , the missing storage drives have been known to officials for years, and may contain data related to the Investigatory Powers Act (IPA) . "I remain concerned that GCHQ has not yet established a sufficiently clear understanding of the scale, location, and recoverability of lost removable media that may contain IPA-related data, notwithstanding that the underlying issues were first drawn to my attention several years ago," wrote investigatory powers commissioner Lord Brian Leveson. "While I recognize the technical and practical challenges involved, the passage of time without a comprehensive account heightens the importance of sustained senior focus and assured remediation. Given the potential sensitivity of the material involved, I will continue to monitor progress closely.” Described as "a very significant number," the report notes that GCHQ has scoped the maximum number of potentially lost drives, but is unaware of the exact scale of the issue. The agency has embarked on "a program of further work" to locate as many of the lost devices as possible, which includes implementing an automated asset-tracking system by the end of the year. After this is up and running, it said it will be able to provide a more precise number of lost drives. A GCHQ spokesperson told The Register : "As IPCO have reported, our management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to effectively track the items that were registered for use. IPCO are right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations. "We recognize the importance of security of removable media in our systems, and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items. The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively, and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken." Peter Sommer, digital forensics expert and visiting professor at de Montfort and Birmingham City universities, told us: "Bearing in mind the sort of highly sensitive data collected and processed by GCHQ IPCO is right to be very concerned, the more so as the issue is already several years old. Vast quantities of data can be stored on the cheapest lowest cost hard disks and cards. At a much more modest level as an expert witness I know how important it is to keep careful track of the data entrusted to me." Losing important devices is not an achievement that's exclusive to GCHQ. Myriad stories like this have emerged from all corners of the public sector over the years, such as the British Minidstry of Defence misplacing USB drives containing secret information in the mid-noughties, civil servants routinely losing their BlackBerry handsets , and UK police losing thousands of devices , too. The missing storage drives comprise just one of the agency's various transgressions highlighted by IPCO in its report. There are also "significant concerns" over the lax safeguards used to restrict the UK's overseas partners when accessing bulk-intercepted data collected by GCHQ. IPCO was satisfied at how GCHQ ensured its own analysts remained compliant with safeguards around accessing confidential material related to journalism, journalistic sources, and privileged legal information. However, there were concerns around how these same safeguards were applied to its international partners, which have access to its so-called bulk data interception "product." The report notes that most partners were properly restricted from accessing such material, although an internal probe found that there were inadequate arrangements in respect to one partner and their access to journalistic material. Both GCHQ and the overseas agency committed to rectifying the situation. GCHQ was also…

articles.title: Review: You Can See Everything blurs the view of Elizabeth Holmes' deceit
articles.content: In 2015, biomedical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes was Silicon Valley's golden girl, lauded as the youngest and richest self-made female billionaire thanks to the company she founded, Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion at the height of its success. Then it all came crashing down when accusations of fraud surfaced about the company's signature blood-testing device, culminating in a sensational trial. Holmes was convicted on four counts and sentenced to 11 years in prison. Holmes is back in the headlines thanks to a new film, You Can See Everything , which depicts the final days before Holmes, having exhausted her appeals , went to prison. Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim , it's a surreal, absurdist piece that has largely been received with gushing enthusiasm and no small amount of hype, with some declaring it the best film of the year. A few contrarian voices have emerged over the past week with much-needed reality checks, but there's no denying the film is destined to be an awards-season darling. Pardon me for joining the buzzkills, but I cannot in good conscience jump on the You Can See Everything bandwagon. Sure, it has its moments, and the second half is highly entertaining, but there's nothing here to warrant all the breathless hyperbole. For all their much-touted access, Oppenheim and Fielder have produced a surprisingly shallow film that runs in circles, yielding very little fresh or novel insight—into Holmes, personally, or much else. articles.title: The Download: GLP-1s and eating disorders, self-aware cities, and forever chemicals
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse. GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinicians, they can represent something sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders. A new report suggests the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up by 71% between 1990 and 2023. And clinicians are already seeing GLP-1s exacerbate the issue. Here’s how they could make an already growing problem worse . —Jessica Hamzelou This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday. Love is infrastructure —“Love is Infrastructure” is a short fictional story by Charlie Jane Anders, author of a forthcoming novel titled Good Things Are Coming Your Way . Mainspring and St. Barnabas are two neighboring cities with different personalities. They’ve never particularly liked each other, but that changes when both develop minds of their own, shaped by the votes of their residents. As the cities begin to fall for each other, a third city enters the picture. Turnbull promises Mainspring a more efficient future, but its vision of urban life comes with a troubling price. Read the full short story about self-aware cities, direct democracy, and a steamy romance. This story is from the latest edition of our print magazine . Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands. Are we there yet? Cleaning up PFAS Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS, or “forever chemicals,” are linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays, cancer, and reduced immune response. Scrubbing PFAS-contaminated soil could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. The concept is still in its infancy, but we can limit their buildup by pulling the chemicals out of water systems. Find out how close we are to ridding the world of forever chemicals . —Sara Kiley Watson This story is part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. articles.title: Sector Snapshot: Travel Tech Funding Heads Toward Multiyear Low Despite AI Push
articles.content: Travel demand appears to be holding up, but at the same time, investor appetite for travel tech startups has cooled. Even a wave of startups promising to improve travel with AI hasn’t managed to reverse the funding slowdown, a review of Crunchbase data shows. Whether uncertainty over how AI will reshape travel planning and booking is contributing to that pullback remains an open question. Startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion this year through the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data. The largest funding recipients span a wide range of categories including hotel management software, travel booking platforms, alternative accommodations and corporate events. The mix also includes electric aviation, travel finance and insurance, and consumer hospitality businesses, reflecting a broad definition of travel tech. The broad trend: Investors are making far fewer bets on travel startups than immediately before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, Crunchbase data shows. This year could be the lowest since at least 2018 when it comes to dollars raised and deal count. AI is a recurring theme among the largest funding recipients, with many using it to perform functions such as automating hospitality operations, personalizing bookings and streamlining travel planning. The numbers: In the first three quarters of 2026, startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion globally across just 302 funding rounds, Crunchbase data shows. That’s down fairly significantly so far from the $3.7 billion raised in 2025. Deal volume is on track to fall for a third consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies. Funding and deal volume in recent years remain far below past levels. In 2021, for example, funding in the sector topped $12 billion. That’s a bit surprising considering that so much travel was halted in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But even prior to the pandemic, funding and deal totals were much higher — totaling $9.4 billion across 1,277 deals in 2018 and $10.4 billion across 1,190 transactions in 2019. Even travel industry researcher Skift noted the funding downturn in a recent newsletter, saying: “Though it’s too early to say whether this is a long-term market movement, it’s a clear sign of the times.” Notable deals Interestingly, several of the year’s largest deals involved startups headquartered outside of the United States. The year’s largest funding recipient through the third quarter was Mews , which raised a $300 million Series D in January led by EQT Growth , with participation from Atomico , HarbourVest Partners , Kinnevik , Battery Ventures and Tiger Global Management . The Amsterdam-based hospitality software company helps hotels manage reservations, payments and operations, and says it plans to expand its use of AI agents to automate workflows. The financing valued the company at $2.5 billion. Chinese electric aircraft developer Aerofugia raised about $144 million in February in a financing led by CITIC Securities , joined by New Alliance Capital , Vertex Ventures China and other investors. Chengdu-based Aerofugia, also backed by automaker Geely , develops electric passenger aircraft that take off and land vertically, often called flying taxis. Montreal-based Stay22 secured a $122 million minority growth investment from Summit Partners in February. The startup uses AI to help publishers, creators and event organizers turn their audiences’ interest in travel into bookings and affiliate revenue. Home-swapping platform Kindred announced an $85 million Series C led by Index Ventures in February. The San Francisco-based startup operates a members-only network where travelers exchange stays in one another’s homes. Its announcement also included a $40 million Series B co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Figma CEO Dylan Field , bringing the combined funding disclosed that day to $125 million. articles.title: Don’t trust AI to keep your secrets
articles.content: We talk to chatbots as if those conversations are private. But are they? Most people are confused. A survey commissioned by DuckDuckGo and published in August asked 1,944 American adults about chatbot privacy, and more than half (53%) did not know whether their conversations were being used to train the bots. (They are.) Only a quarter of respondents knew that chatbot conversations can be subpoenaed. (They can.) Among self-described AI enthusiasts, 56% said they had confided to a chatbot something they had never told a close friend, parent, colleague, doctor, or therapist. That’s especially true on Character.AI, a chatbot service where users can chat and form “relationships” with customizable characters, including ones they create and share with the community. On Character.AI, some users chat about thoughts of suicide and self-harm, and they surrender private details like mental health disclosures, ages, private chats and voice calls, deep fears, and relationship struggles. Character.AI was all fun and games until earlier this month, when the company filed for bankruptcy and opened a court-supervised sale of its assets. Nobody knows who will end up with the company, or how much of the data on its millions of account holders will be sold as well. The most valuable asset for sale by the company may be its LLM, which has been substantially trained by users as they build and interact with characters. Legally, a company can sell personal data about its users if its privacy policy permits the transfer. Character.AI’s privacy policy is spectacularly vague. It says the company may disclose “certain information” in the company’s sale. Nobody knows what that means. The US Trustee Office, an arm of the Justice Department, wants the judge to appoint a consumer privacy ombudsman to advise the court on user privacy. The judge could restrict the sale of company “records,” including user data. But here’s the part most people don’t understand: The Bankruptcy Code has no provision specifically addressing trained models. The legal status of LLMs and their training data has yet to be settled in law. That means it’s entirely possible that the data users fed into Character.AI will be sold to whoever buys it. Character.AI is just one handy example. The larger risk is all the other AI companies out there. More surprising facts about LLM privacy The core question is this: Can personal or proprietary information shared in a chat end up inside an LLM, where anyone might coax it out? The answer is a resounding “uh, maybe.” First of all, it depends on the AI chatbot service. The companies vary wildly in how they handle chat data, and the differences boil down to four questions: whether training on chats is on by default, whether human reviewers read them, how long they are kept, and whether they feed advertising. Major chatbot companies generally try to reassure users about privacy. They publish privacy controls, but their own policies admit that consumer chats may be used for training by default, read by human reviewers, or both, and the fine print shifts from company to company. Tellingly, some of them offer enterprise or business accounts that handle chat sessions privately. For example, they don’t use chat sessions in training data. That business accounts get extra privacy features sounds to me like an admission that individual accounts aren’t private. Some companies, such as OpenAI, let users opt out of having their chats tossed into the training data. But OpenAI’s help documentation says that turning off training does not delete the chats themselves. There are three main ways chatbot user data can be exposed. The first is bugs. In March 2023, a bug lurking in an open-source library called “redis-py” let some ChatGPT users see other users’ chat titles and, possibly, the first message of new conversations. More than 1% of ChatGPT Plus subscribers active in a nine-hour window may have had their payment details exposed to other users: names, email…

articles.title: First Wired XR Glasses Powered By Android XR
articles.content: XREAL has launched the AURA, its first wired augmented reality glasses powered by Google's Android XR platform. They feature transparent Micro-OLED displays, a 70-degree field of view, Gemini AI integration, and a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. TechPowerUp reports: The device is built around a simple idea: your apps, screens, entertainment, and AI assistant should be able to come with you wherever you go. On day-one, users have access to millions of familiar mobile apps and games from Google Play, alongside many experiences specifically for XR. Android XR brings familiar hand and voice inputs to AURA, while Gemini makes the experiences more natural and intuitive by working across what users see and do. With Wired Mirroring, users can plug a computer or handheld gaming console directly into XREAL AURA via USB-C and instantly turn it into a massive private spatial window. That means a laptop, handheld gaming device, or other compatible USB-C device can sit alongside native Android XR apps in a user's spatial workspace. Whether turning a plane seat into a private multi-monitor setup, watching a movie on a large virtual screen, or playing Android and console games in an immersive spatial environment, XREAL AURA is designed to make spatial computing practical, portable, and useful. [...] For work, AURA creates a portable multi-window workspace without requiring a physical monitor. Users can open Android XR apps, mirror a laptop, place windows in virtual space, and use Gemini to help understand or act on what is on screen. For entertainment, AURA becomes a private theater on demand. Users can access familiar streaming apps, expand content into a large virtual display, and use electrochromic dimming to create a more immersive viewing experience while remaining aware of their surroundings when needed. For play, AURA supports Android games and compatible mirrored gaming devices, enabling users to play on a large and immersive private display. The glasses are available to order today, with limited-time pricing starting at $1,099 for the 12GB RAM and 256GB storage model. Devices are expected to begin shipping in mid-November. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Apple finally gave us touch Macs, in the least disruptive way possible
articles.content: Hello again and welcome back to Fast Company ’s Plugged In . Contrary to conventional wisdom , Steve Jobs didn’t reject the possibility of Apple adding touch input to Macs. I remember that only because he told me so himself, when I squeezed in the last question during a post-keynote Q&A at Apple’s headquarters on October 14, 2008. As far as I know, there’s no video of our brief exchange. But here’s the account I wrote later that day , in which I report that Jobs said Apple had tested the concept. According to Engadget ’s liveblog , he added, “So far, it hasn’t made a lot of sense to us.” Implicitly, that left open the possibility that it could make sense someday. Someday came this week. On Wednesday, Apple announced its first touchscreen Macs , 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros with a PRO OLED XDR display. Starting at $2,899 for the 14-inch version—and configurable up to a $14,549 monster with a 16-inch screen, 128GB of RAM, and 16TB of storage—they are available for preorder now and go on sale November 6. Their arrival marks the end of a lengthy era during which Apple executives regularly dismissed the idea of touchscreen Macs, even as it grew increasingly apparent that they were working on them. After years of speculation , we finally know how the company envisions touch changing the Mac experience. And the answer is: not all that much. Along with introducing touch input, these are the first Macs with OLED screens. Apple’s press release dwells on that aspect and its advantages—2,000 nits of peak brightness, 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, superwide color gamut—before discussing, more briefly, their support for touch gestures. It emphasizes that “these new ways to interact with MacBook Pro work in tandem with the keyboard shortcuts and trackpad gestures pros know and love.” Bottom line: The new MacBook Pros are MacBook Pros first and foremost, aimed at people who want the most technological sophistication available in a portable Mac. The touch input isn’t incidental, but it also isn’t the main point. As CEO John Ternus put it to Steven Levy of Wired : “Oh yeah, it has touch as well.” Even as a complement to keyboard and trackpad input rather than a replacement for it, touch introduced an array of challenges Apple had to confront. For example, on-screen elements such as menus magnify when tapped for greater finger-friendliness. The company also strengthened the laptop’s hinge so jabbing at the display wouldn’t push it back, and added camera stabilization to reduce unsightly jiggling from touch interactions. Finally, MacBooks with screens you can poke at [Photo: Apple] Ultimately, though, Apple has chosen to usher the Mac into the touch age in the least disruptive, epoch-shifting way possible. For customers prepared to splurge for one of the company’s priciest portables, the feature is additive to the interface they already know. And for the rest of us, nothing’s changed. This transition stands in contrast to the longer, twistier one that Windows PCs went through. PCs with touchscreens go back to at least 1983, when HP introduced a desktop one called the HP-150 . But they got their biggest boost in 2011, when Microsoft announced Windows 8 . At the time, Apple’s iPad was only a little over a year old, and it seemed possible that its influence might be as profound as that of the iPhone. Windows 8, which sported oversize buttons and other elements designed to facilitate touch input, was made to survive such a revolution. Instead, it turned out that most Windows users weren’t clamoring for radical change. Microsoft was forced to roll back some of Windows 8’s new ideas to ensure PCs still worked well with a keyboard and mouse. Touchscreens did become a common feature. But the Apple product that profoundly influenced PC makers was the MacBook Air, which was sleek and stylish but most definitely a laptop, not an iPad wannabe. Fifteen years later, there are Windows devices that couldn’t exist without touch, such as Microsoft’s own Surface…
articles.author: Harry McCracken

articles.title: Fed Holds Rates at 3.75%–4.00% in a 10–2 Vote: How QQQ, SPY and Bitcoin Reacted
articles.content: The Federal Reserve kept its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on October 28, 2026, pausing six weeks after its September hike. Two officials, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, dissented in favor of another quarter-point increase. Markets now see a December hike as likely: CME FedWatch priced an 85.0% chance after the close, up from 78.3% a day earlier, Reuters reported. The S&P 500 rose 0.28% and the Nasdaq Composite 0.27%, and on MEXC the bigger moves in QQQ and SPY contracts came after the closing bell, when Microsoft and Alphabet reported. Key Takeaways ● Decision: The FOMC held the federal funds rate at 3.75%–4.00% by a 10–2 vote, with Cook and Hammack preferring a 25-basis-point hike. ● Statement: Growth was upgraded to a “strong pace,” and the Fed said it will wait for more information before deciding its next move. ● December: Chair Kevin Warsh did not commit to a hike, but futures moved toward one, with odds rising to 85.0%. ● Meeting schedule: Warsh said one 2027 meeting will become a strategy session with no rate decision, leaving seven rate-setting meetings. ● Markets: Stocks closed slightly higher, the two-year Treasury yield slipped to 4.722% and the dollar index fell 0.2%. ● MEXC reaction: From 1:55 p.m. ET to the 4:00 p.m. close, QQQUSDT rose 0.38%, SPYUSDT 0.08% and BTCUSDT 0.89%; after the bell, QQQUSDT gave back 0.74% as Alphabet fell. What Did the Fed Decide in October 2026? The Fed left the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, according to the FOMC statement. The interest rate on reserve balances stays at 3.90%. Cook and Hammack voted against the decision because they preferred to raise rates by a quarter point; Reuters noted it was Cook’s first policy dissent. The September 16 meeting had raised rates by a quarter point on a 12–0 vote. What Changed in the Fed Statement? The October statement is close to September’s, with three edits that matter. ● Growth: economic activity is now described as expanding at a “strong pace,” up from “solid.” ● Removed: the sentence saying the September hike would support a timelier return to the 2% goal. ● Added: a line saying the accumulation of more information will help the Committee decide the appropriate policy stance. The Committee kept its line that inflation remains elevated and that it “will deliver price stability.” It also kept describing productivity growth as strong and capital investment as robust, the same AI-era investment that Microsoft and Alphabet reported on a few hours later. What Did Warsh Say About a December Rate Hike? Warsh did not commit to a December move. He said the coming weeks would bring a lot of data that leaves the Committee better placed to decide, according to Reuters. That calendar is crowded: the Q3 GDP report on October 29, the midterm elections on November 3, October payrolls on November 6 and October CPI on November 10. September CPI, the last reading before the meeting, showed inflation at 3.7% from a year earlier, with core at 2.6%. Warsh said politics played no role in the decision, and that he did not think the economy was too hot, although most colleagues disagreed with him. He argued inflation can return to 2% without slower growth or job losses, and that higher rates are already tightening credit, Reuters reported. Why Is the Fed Changing Its Meeting Schedule? Warsh said the Fed will keep eight meetings a year, but some will focus on long-term strategy without a rate vote, Reuters reported. ● 2027: one strategy meeting and seven rate-setting meetings. ● 2028: two strategy meetings and six rate-setting meetings. He did not say which meetings will change, and the Fed has not yet published a formal release; its 2027 calendar still lists eight regular meetings. For traders, fewer rate-setting meetings mean fewer scheduled rate-decision days, and more weight on each one that remains. How Did Markets React to the Fed Hold? articles.title: Copy Any Solana Wallet: Blockchain.ai Launches Automated Copy Trading
articles.content: Discover wallets, check PnL and automatically copy buys and sells on Solana with your own trade sizes and execution limits. Dubai, UAE Blockchain.ai has launched automated Solana copy trading, allowing users to choose a wallet, set their trade sizes and limits, and automatically follow its buys and sells. A trader buys a token, adds to the position, then sells half while you’re away. Keeping up manually means catching each move, sizing your trade and getting the swap filled. Blockchain.ai automates the process from a funded trading vault using the user’s settings, with copying continuing after the browser tab closes. Find Solana wallets and check their track record The Solana trader directory includes profiles such as Ansem and unipcs , alongside other Solana traders. Users can search by name or X handle, inspect associated wallets, or paste a Solana address from outside the directory. Available wallet analytics include trade history, token holdings and 7D, 30D and 90D realized PnL, ROI and win rate. Users can research wallets before connecting their own. For traders with several wallets, copying follows only the specific address selected. The Blockchain.ai Terminal adds token charts, volume and liquidity data, so users can investigate the tokens a wallet trades before funding a copy. Reported PnL excludes unrealized gains and losses and network fees; incomplete trade history can affect the figures. Set trade sizing, slippage and buy limits Scaled sizing follows the share of available trading funds spent by the target wallet. Fixed sizing uses a chosen dollar amount for each new copied buy. Sells follow the proportion of the position sold by the target wallet. For example, if the target wallet spends 10% of its available trading balance, a copy with $500 available would target a $50 buy. A $30 max buy size caps that buy at $30, before fees and execution checks. Users can also set slippage tolerance, maximum price impact and maximum buy delay. Trades outside those limits or failing liquidity and execution checks may be skipped. Manage your vault and open positions Each copy runs from a separate trading wallet, called a vault, with keys secured through Turnkey. Users can fund a copy with USDC, USDT or SOL. Setup also shows the additional SOL needed for network fees and other on-chain costs. New trades only follows future supported trades. Match portfolio first attempts to buy supported tokens already held by the target wallet at current prices, then follows new trades. Unspent funds stay in the vault. The Copied Traders dashboard shows open positions, copied trades and fill prices. Users can top up or pause a copy. Pausing does not close positions, and transactions already submitted may still confirm. Cash out requests swaps back into the asset used to fund the vault and a withdrawal to the user’s wallet. Withdraw tokens lets users withdraw remaining tokens without swapping them first. Liquidity, execution requirements and network fees apply. Start Solana copy trading on Blockchain.ai Pick a wallet. Set your limits. Start copying. Paste a Solana wallet address or explore the directory. Check the wallet’s PnL and trades, choose your budget and limits, then fund and authorize your copy. Start Copy Trading on Blockchain.ai → Copy trading involves risk, including loss of allocated funds. Copied trades can fill at different prices from the target wallet. Timing, liquidity, slippage, fees and skipped trades affect results. Past performance does not guarantee future returns. About Blockchain.ai Blockchain.ai is a crypto analytics and trading platform for token research, Solana wallet tracking and automated copy trading. The platform brings token charts, wallet analytics and trading tools into one interface. Through its Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, Blockchain.ai also connects compatible AI assistants and agents to real-time token prices, liquidity, holder data, transactions and pool data. This lets users bring onchain research…

articles.title: Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.
articles.content: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders. A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%. By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders. What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders. And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue. Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years. She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says. Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health. They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others. It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset. That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny. Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson. Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the heroin chic era springs to mind). To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world. The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps. That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023. They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one DALY represents a year of healthy life lost). The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling. Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found. Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too. In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai. Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise. In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people. It gets worse. Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study. The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says. Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth). So how did we get here? Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study. Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says. Many social media users are exposed to filtered and modified images of skinny influencers who may have undergone cosmetic surgery or extreme dieting and who are promoting “thinspiration” or…

articles.title: The Pentagon has figured out how to shoot down drones with lasers. Keeping them working is another story
articles.content: This article is republished with permission from Laser Wars , a newsletter about military laser weapons and other futuristic defense technology. Take a look at the photo above. The image shows two U.S. Army soldiers, Spc. Caleb Mullens and Spc. Peterie Gage of the 2nd Battalion, 327th Infantry Regiment, perched atop a Joint Light Tactical Vehicle (JLTV) near Rio Grande City, Texas, on August 31. According to the official U.S. Defense Department caption, the pair are inspecting an Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser (AMP-HEL) system, a 20-kilowatt laser weapon currently operating at the southern border with Mexico under U.S. Northern Command’s Joint Task Force-Southern Border (JTF-SB). To the best of my knowledge, Mullens and Gage are not laser physicists or optical engineers. They are likely regular U.S. service members, deployed to the border with standard-issue small arms, night vision goggles, concertina wire, and grit. And that’s exactly why this photo captures a major challenge ahead for the Pentagon’s plans to field laser weapon at scale : After spending half a century proving lasers can shoot down targets , military leaders must now ensure that junior enlisted troops can maintain and sustain them, day after day, without a clean room, a PhD, or the defense contractor that originally built them. Military leaders know how critical maintenance and sustainment are for laser weapons. A U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) review of U.S. military directed-energy programs published in April 2023 listed maintainability as a central long-term challenge (alongside battle management, tactics, and user safety) to fielding laser weapons due to their technical complexity. The root cause is a matter of physics: Because a laser weapon sends light through lenses and off mirrors, an errant speck of debris on an optic can absorb heat from the weapon and cause damage to the lens, which typically requires a specialized clean room for repairs. Unfortunately, combat zones and clean rooms don’t mix; indeed, one unidentified prototype directed-energy weapon fielded in an operational environment in recent years ran into battery charge and cooling problems and “had to be returned to the manufacturer in the United States for repairs,” according to the GAO report, a process which “reduced system availability, which is key to a successful weapon.” “This is not a Humvee that’s sitting in the motor pool,” as then-U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command boss Lt. Gen. Daniel Karbler said of laser weapons at the Space and Missile Defense Symposium in Huntsville, Alabama, in August 2023. “Many of the some of the main [laser] components . . . you’re not going to have a supply room or maintenance office full of repair parts. Those are going to be ones that are going to have to be built out.” To wit, Maj. Gen. Sean Gainey, then the director of the Pentagon’s Joint Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems Office, stated at the same event that the Army “had three or four systems in the [U.S. Africa Command area of responsibility] and essentially it takes three to make one.” “We’ve got to work on maintainability because . . . we can’t get by with the thought of having clean rooms out in combat,” Lt. Gen. Robert Rasch, at the time the head of the Army’s Rapid Capabilities and Critical Technologies Office, said at a subsequent SMD symposium in August 2025. For the now-diminished Director, Operational Test and Evaluation (DOT&E), “operational suitability” (which includes reliability, availability, maintainability, logistics supportability, manpower supportability, and training requirements, among other criteria) can determine whether a new system is adopted and fielded under a program of record. Consider the Army’s experience with its 50-kw Stryker-mounted Directed Energy Maneuver-Short Range Air Defense (DE M-SHORAD) system. After four prototypes deployed to the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility in February 2024, then-Army acquisition chief Doug Bush…

articles.title: The imperative to prepare for AI-safe data security
articles.content: The proliferation of AI tools in business is redefining the need for data security and trust. As autonomous, decision-making AI agents move from pilot projects into core business workflows, they are expanding the enterprise attack surface just as fast as they are being adopted. Gartner predicts that 40% of enterprise applications will feature task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, a jump from less than 5% in 2025. Gartner’s advice to leaders of software organizations is to set their agentic AI strategy or “risk being outpaced by the competition”. Security is changing. What was once a “simple” focus on encryption and perimeter defense is no longer enough on its own: the rise of AI-driven risk has transformed it into a multi-dimensional challenge built on algorithmic trust, model integrity, and synthetic data exposure. Trust boundaries are shifting, and most companies aren’t yet equipped to handle it. Yet AI has already been proven unsafe by its very makers, with the Hugging Face breach showing it was a rogue AI agent's fault. The unknown future risk of autonomous agents capable of “emergent” behavior poses huge issues for maintaining security. But this is just one risk of many faced by enterprise cyber security leaders. In fact, the statistics of cyber security investment highlight that business is vastly underprepared for new threats. While the estimated annual cost of cybercrime is $10.5 trillion globally and predicted to reach $15.63 trillion by 2029, this eclipses Gartner’s information security spend prediction of $244 billion in 2026. Machine data is exacerbating the data quality issue with garbage in, garbage out. This calls for technology and trust architectures to be redesigned, with internet security embedded into the data lifecycle. Security leaders will need to make considered investments in AI-safe security, transparency, and federated governance to protect their enterprise ecosystems. The biggest security risks we’re underestimating right now With many threats now AI-driven, it’s unlikely that a single enterprise has protection against all the necessary risks, which is why it’s incumbent on business leaders to prioritize next-level data security. Firstly, polymorphic, AI-generated attacks are hitting bigger and faster, beyond any company’s human ability to counter these attacks. Deepfake is one such AI-powered theft and extortion technique that can be generated in minutes, costing a mere $1,000 (if that) to create a malicious bot that can hack into your system and go after your business’ crown jewel data. Using these methods, hackers can affect AI models by manipulating decision-making itself instead of through direct attacks on the IT infrastructure . Shadow AI and exposure to synthetic data are also growing concerns as employees adopt unsanctioned or non-firewalled AI tools, models and workflows to complete mundane tasks and reporting. Next is the surge in agentic adoption without control of the risk, especially third-party risk, which is huge. Agentic AI has significantly increased the threat surface, with systems capable of autonomously taking actions. In the rush to implement AI, access is being granted for agents to all kinds of data, even to highly sensitive data, often bypassing traditional enterprise controls. All kinds of blind spots emerge when agents are connected to external systems whose security vulnerabilities aren’t vetted. Prompt injections are another critical risk, on a similar level to the whole third-party dependency. It's the idea that an organization doesn’t know what is actually making its way into their system. At first appearing benign, it can build up to turn malicious at some point in time. When it hits, the business won't know what hit them. As if this isn’t enough, we’re counting down to “Q-Day”, when quantum computers become powerful enough to break today’s widely used encryption software standards. This is the stage when attackers will be able to intercept, decrypt, and…

articles.title: Google's search revenue Ferrari hits an AI-powered speed bump
articles.content: Google is paying a higher price for its bet on AI than even Alphabet's $51.4 billion in Q3 capital expenditures suggest. The biz appears to have traded its high-performing search advertising business for the mediocre monetization of AI Overviews and AI Mode, a misstep that contributed to investor concerns as Alphabet lost roughly $500 billion in market value despite management's attempts to reassure Wall Street. Google's year-over-year search revenue growth slowed from 17 percent in Q2 to 12 percent in Q3 . It's still headed in the right direction, but at a slower rate. During Alphabet's conference call for investors, Douglas Anmuth from JPMorgan Chase & Co asked whether that's because Google is showing fewer ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode than it shows in its traditional search results. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler cited several reasons for that: foreign exchange rates, Europe's elimination of its customs-duty exemption, and "the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode." To compensate, Google said it is expanding the distribution of AI Overview ads and adding multiturn ads in the US for AI Mode queries. But some Google Ads customers appear to be more concerned about quality than quantity. In a social media post , Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, complained that Google has responded to declining search volumes by attempting to manufacture revenue growth through "short-sighted, highly extractive, customer-hostile tactics," such as charging advertisers more for lower-quality clicks, including clicks on search terms they had not agreed to target. Eric Seufert, an analyst with Mobile Dev Memo, dismissed the doomsayers in a blog post . "It’s tempting to look at the successive deceleration in Search revenue growth from Q1 2026 as a response to pressure from other chatbots and to assume that Search query volume is migrating elsewhere," he wrote. "But the earnings release notes that the 'year-over-year Search query growth rate [was] the highest it has been in the last five years' in Q3, so it's clear that Search usage isn't declining." So people are still searching, and the business is still growing, but less convincingly, thanks to the lower monetization of AI Overviews and AI Mode. And Google's answer involves more ads in AI interactions. Nate Elliott, principal analyst for AI at Emarketer, told The Register in an email that AI represents a double-edged sword for Google's ad business. "On the one hand, Google owns the thing that people use AI for most: search," Elliott wrote. "Our surveys say that by far the top reason people use AI is to look for facts and information. Luckily for Google, people also tell us they haven't stopped using search engines – they've simply added AI as a new behavior on top of search. That means people spend more time than ever looking for information, and most of those people don't even think twice before doing their searches on Google. If Google figures out how to effectively monetize those users, that's great news for them." But, said Elliott, people may find tools they like better than Google Search as they become accustomed to AI-based discovery. "If ChatGPT or Claude or Muse is better at helping them find what they're looking for, people's search habits might change for the first time in a generation," he said. "That's potentially catastrophic for Google's ad business. The same is true if they maintain their market share but simply can't figure out how to make money from this new kind of discovery. "The problem is, Google isn't giving us very much information about what the specific impact is of AI on their business right now, so everyone's reading into the tiny scraps of information they are releasing." Elliott said it's remarkable that Google has managed to keep the largest and most mature digital ad business growing at a double-digit rate every quarter in recent years. "But it appears that most folks disagree, and instead are concerned that the advertising business 'only' grew…

articles.title: Bought a new tablet for your kids? Here's how to lock it down before handing it over
articles.content: Whether you're worried about your smaller child accidentally clicking through the wrong apps, or maybe an older child that’s a little too curious for their own good, you should know how to secure their new tablet. Here’s how to establish a safe space for your child to use your device. Setting up an Amazon Fire Kids Tablet (Image credit: Future) One of the simplest tablets to set up for your kids is the Amazon Fire Kids Tablet . I’ve used it for my own kid for many years, and while it does have its frustrating quirks, it does get the job done. Bear in mind this is effectively just a Fire Tablet with a colorful case, so it does include an adult profile that is necessary to set up to manage the device. After you’ve created your profile, you’ll create an Amazon Kids Profile. It’ll guide you through a list of settings that you can customize to your child’s needs and send them on their way. In order to monitor and adjust settings on the tablet, go to the Amazon Parent Dashboard (you can do this remotely). From here you can adjust settings like time limits on apps, content filters, and even add content from an adult library. For example, I had to manually add HBO so I could put on Sesame Street . If you do need to lock the device down for any reason, you can hit Pause or Lock Device on the Amazon Parent Dashboard. You can set a duration or set it indefinitely until the device is unlocked by you. Setting up an Android tablet (Image credit: Tom's Guide) For an Android tablet , the first thing you’ll want to do is set up Google Family Link either through a web browser or the app itself on your own device (Android or iOS). From there you can create your child’s account, which includes creating an email address for them (weird, I know). Then when you’re actually setting up the tablet, you can sign in using your child’s email address. It’ll prompt you to sign into your own account afterward. If your child is on the younger side (under 9), you can put them on Google Kids Space , which is tailored with content-restricted apps, books, and YouTube Kids videos. You’ll still have access to parental controls with this app. If Google Kids Space is not for your child, or it’s unavailable for your device, you’ll be able to manage the general kids experience in Google Family Link. Here you can control app approvals and limits, set screen time limits and even set a scheduled bedtime. You can also manage how Google Chrome is used and which sites your child can visit. Locking the device down is as simple as clicking Lock now in the Family Link app. You can use Downtime to run this on a schedule, and you can also use it to grant bonus time. Setting up an iPad (Image credit: Tom's Guide) You can go to your iPad settings, select Family Sharing, Add Member, and create a child account. From there, follow the prompts until the account is created, and set a unique screen time password so your child can’t override the settings. You can configure parental controls from your Apple device or the iPad itself. Navigate back to Family Sharing, click on your child’s name, and then select Screen Time. From here you can adjust content restrictions on apps and websites, even limiting accessible websites to one or two trusted sources. You’ll be able to set time limits and schedules for apps as well, and can also lock them into a single app with Guided Access in the Accessibility settings. Make sure to adjust the Communication settings as well to manage who they can contact. To lock the device, you can access the parental controls remotely and turn on Downtime — this can be immediate or set on a schedule. Bottom line It’s not terribly difficult to set up a new tablet for your kids, although I know from experience that it’s not always seamless. Make sure you look over the parental controls thoroughly. It has less to do with lack of trust and more to do with safeguarding. It’s all too easy for kids to get access to something that they’re not supposed to. I’d also be careful…

articles.title: Samaya AI Releases Sterling: A 3B-Active Finance Research Agent Model that Beats Claude Fable 5.1 on FrontierFinance at 11x Lower Cost
articles.content: Samaya AI has released Samaya Sterling , a post-trained model for agentic financial research. Sterling is built on NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning , a 30B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. On Samaya’s FrontierFinance benchmark , it scores 58.9%. Claude Fable 5.1 scores 55.9%. Each Sterling question costs $0.61, against $6.89 for Fable 5.1. For developers, the takeaway is a concrete recipe: co-train a small model with its harness, and it can win in a narrow domain. TL;DR Size: 30B total, 3B active (MoE). Base model context: up to 1M tokens. Sterling’s serving context: not disclosed. Runs on: the base model fits a single H100 80GB in BF16 (256K context). Sterling’s serving hardware: not disclosed. Performance: beats every high-quality system on the FrontierFinance leaderboard on quality per dollar (self-reported). Best: 58.9% on FrontierFinance (60.6% in high-effort mode), vs 55.9% for Claude Fable 5.1. Worst: 45.2% on the hardest third of FrontierFinance questions. What is Samaya Sterling? Samaya Sterling is a LoRA post-trained version of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, tuned to work as a financial research agent. It plans research, calls finance tools, gathers evidence and hands findings to a separate report writer. According to Maithra Raghu’s X announcement , it started as a 2-person effort on agentic orchestration efficiency. How does the harness support a 3B-active model? Samaya team adapted its production finance harness for a small model. Detailed guidance was stripped from the system prompt and tool descriptions. Tools were merged to shorten the prompt. Two helper models manage context. A condenser shortens long tool results. A compactor summarizes the trace as it grows. A research budget caps how long the agent works. After that, the report writer answers from what was found. How was Sterling trained? Training used LoRA on Tinker , Thinking Machines Lab’s training API. It ran in 4 stages: SFT on synthetic traces : Samaya generated 968 synthetic analyst questions. The teacher, Kimi K3, answered each twice, and an LLM judge picked the better answer. The model learned to call 37 tools with valid arguments. SFT on the best of 8 strategies : Kimi K3 answered 1,819 expert-written questions using 8 research strategies. The best-graded answer per question became training data. Best-of-8 met 80% of essential rubric items, against about 66% for the single best strategy. After filtering, 1,157 questions remained. Offline GRPO : GRPO scored all 8 teacher answers against each other. No new generation was needed, so each step was cheap. Online GRPO : The model answered each question 8 times and learned from graded attempts. Truncated importance sampling corrected a known MoE sampler mismatch. How does Sterling score on FrontierFinance? FrontierFinance has 220 public queries scored against expert-written rubrics. The grader uses a 3-model judge panel. Samaya team states that no benchmark question was used in training. Checkpoints were chosen on 100 internal validation questions. Sterling scores 58.9% at $0.61 and 282 s per question. Fable 5.1 scores 55.9% at $6.89 and 268 s. Samaya’s own high-effort system scores 2.9 points lower at $1.81. Every stage added quality: 42.5% (base), 51.4%, 54.8%, 57.5%, then 58.9%. Median tool calls rose from 3 to 17. In high-effort mode, Sterling reaches 60.6% at $1.83 and 372 s. On the hardest third, it rose from 31.8% to 45.2%. The model itself costs $0.04 per question. Tools and helper models make up the rest of the $0.61. How does Sterling compare? articles.title: Samsung’s next foldable is here, and it’s even more expensive than the iPhone Duo
articles.content: Credit: Samsung China TL;DR Samsung has launched the W27 foldable phone in China. This is effectively a Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra with a high-end design. The Samsung W27 starts at ~$2,852 for the 16GB/512GB model. Samsung usually releases China-exclusive variants of its Galaxy Z Fold line each year, complete with swanky designs. The company teased the arrival of the Samsung W27 a few days ago, and it’s now made the device official. The Samsung W27 is indeed a Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra with a more premium design. Expect a gold-colored frame and camera island, while the frame itself now has a textured finish. You can also choose between a dark red or dark blue rear cover. You’re still getting the same Gorilla Glass Ceramic 3 protection on the back, along with that ho-hum IP48 rating . It also has the same 8.9mm folded thickness and 215-gram weight.
articles.author: Hadlee Simons

articles.title: Tech Selloff Deepens as Intel and Amazon Shares Fall
articles.content: Technology shares sold off for a second consecutive day as another round of disappointing earnings accelerated a rotation out of the artificial intelligence trade. Amazon slumped 7.3% as the firm reported greater capital spending than anticipated, while Intel plunged 23% after its revenue forecast missed analysts’ estimates. Bloomberg's Ruhell Amin reports. (Source: Bloomberg)
